```{r setup}
if (basename(getwd()) == "manuscript") {
  root <- normalizePath(file.path(getwd(), ".."))
} else {
  root <- normalizePath(getwd())
}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = root)

show_fig <- function(path, caption, alt, id, width = NULL) {
  # `caption` is the full, visible figure caption (becomes the figure's
  # caption text via pandoc's implicit-figure handling). `alt` is a
  # short, separate description for screen readers, passed through via
  # pandoc's image `{alt="..."}` attribute, per UNR's own accessibility
  # guidance, alt text should be succinct (roughly under 150 characters),
  # while the full descriptive caption stays as real, visible text.
  # `id` sets the figure's Quarto crossref id (e.g. "fig-timeline"), so
  # it renders as a numbered "Figure N" and can be cited by number via
  # @id in the prose. `width` (e.g. "55%") constrains the rendered
  # width -- needed for a handful of naturally very tall (portrait)
  # source images, which otherwise scale to the full text width and
  # overflow past the bottom margin in the PDF/LaTeX output (confirmed
  # directly: an unconstrained tall image pushed its own caption text
  # into the page-number footer).
  abs_path <- file.path(normalizePath(getwd()), path)
  abs_path <- gsub("\\\\", "/", abs_path)
  alt_escaped <- gsub('"', "'", alt)
  width_attr <- if (is.null(width)) "" else sprintf(' width="%s"', width)
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf('![%s](%s){#%s fig-alt="%s"%s}', caption, abs_path, id, alt_escaped, width_attr))
}
```

# Project overview and roadmap {.unnumbered}

**What this thesis is about.** In June 2025 an old capped pipe on the Lower Sinter Terrace at Steamboat Hills, just south of Reno, erupted, and since then thermal water has been coming out at new vents, springs and seeps across the terrace. Nobody knows yet whether this is a change in the deep system or the same plumbing finding new routes to the surface. The thermal water that leaves the system ends up in Steamboat Creek, and the usual way to track it is to measure chloride, which is high in the thermal water and low in everything else. Chloride needs a laboratory sample, so it has been measured only a few times in seventy years. The main question of the thesis is whether specific conductance, which a logger records every few minutes, can stand in for chloride, so that thermal outflow can be followed continuously. A second line of work uses geochemical modeling of the springs, wells and fissure gas to check that the proxy is chemically sound and to describe how the fluid changes between the fissure and the creek. The work starts at the fissure and moves outward: the terrace's own discharge points, then the creek, then the wider monitoring network of production, injection, monitoring and domestic wells.

**Guiding questions.**

1. How stable is the chloride-conductivity relationship through time and across site types (RQ1)?
2. What is the minimum chloride-sampling frequency that keeps a conductivity-based flux estimate defensible (RQ2)?
3. Is conductance driven by conservative mixing or by reactions that decouple it from chloride (RQ3)?
4. Has geothermal outflow changed since the eruption (RQ4)?
5. Where does heat reach the surface at the terrace, which discharge points share a source, and how much of the creek's thermal inflow is pumped resort water?

**Approach.** The data come from one database that combines my field samples and loggers, NDEP and other agency records, USGS discharge, and chemistry transcribed from the older papers. The proxy is tested with paired chloride and conductance samples from December through September, with a Monte Carlo analysis setting how often to sample. PHREEQC and mixing models check the chemistry and follow the fluid from the fissure to the creek. A georeferenced thermal map and mapped fissures and faults give the surface picture of the Lower Terrace. Possible further work includes resistivity lines with Christopher Kratt (UNR), if the landowners allow, and a Leapfrog model of the wells, faults and fissures. Collaborators are Cary Lindsey, Owen Callahan and Rachel Micander (NBMG), Phil Busick and Gene Savoy for Lower Terrace history and access, and Ormat, if an agreement is possible.

**From question to answer.** @tbl-qa lines up each question with the data that bear on it, the method, the product, and what result would change the interpretation.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\footnotesize
```

| Question | Data | Method | Product | What would change the answer |
|----------|----------------|-----------------|----------------|------------------|
| RQ1: stability of the chloride-conductance relation | Paired chloride and conductance samples over about ten months (December to September); logger record | Log-linear and additive regression compared with a random forest, scored with time-ordered cross-validation | Calibration equation or equations with uncertainty, by site type | Residuals that grow in one season or differ between the two stations, which would call for site-specific equations |
| RQ2: sampling frequency | Conductance records at SBRR and SBGG | Monte Carlo subsampling at 1 to 14 day intervals | Recommended interval with an error bound | A mass-flux error, once discharge overlaps the loggers, much larger than the conductance error |
| RQ3: conservative mixing or reaction | NDEP, field and historical chemistry; fissure gas | PHREEQC speciation, mixing, reaction paths and inverse models; principal components; Leapfrog compartments | Test of chloride and conductance behavior; end-member set; candidate reactions | Non-conservative chloride, or carbonate and sulfate reactions strong enough to break the conductance-chloride link |
| RQ4: change in outflow | Chloride fluxes, discharge, tracer ratios, thermal map | Chloride balance with stated uncertainty; Cl/B ratio; heat check | Post-eruption discharge and a comparison with the 70-year record | A shift in Cl/B, or discharge outside the 1955-2016 range after uncertainty is counted |
| Lower Terrace sources and the resort | Thermal map, fissure and spring points, resort tank logger, resort flow | Polygon attribution, source-stratified sampling, share of the thermal inflow | Map of heat sources; resort share with a measured rate | A measured resort flow outside the 1 to 18 percent bracket |

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

**Why it matters.** The thermal discharge of Steamboat Creek has been estimated only a handful of times in 70 years, each time from a campaign of chloride samples and gauge readings. If conductance can be calibrated against chloride, a logger can supply that record continuously, and the 2025 eruption becomes the first event at Steamboat whose aftermath is tracked at that resolution. The work gives regulators and operators a cheap way to check outflow, and it gives the owners of the Lower Terrace a documented account of what is changing.


**Work completed to date.** The database holds more than 1,650 samples and about 380 wells plus several hundred located springs, seeps and creek sites. PHREEQC speciation is done for 404 samples, with mixing, reaction-path and gas results for the terrace flowpath. Three fissure gas samples are air-corrected and compared with Mariner and Janik's 1995 data. The chloride balance for 1 May 2026 gives 58.65 L/s of thermal inflow, and the thermal map gives 488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius, attributed to resort infrastructure, the fissure zone, the Lower Terrace channel and creek-corridor springs. Leapfrog input files exist for 236 wells, and the Monte Carlo test has been run on the measured conductance record.

**How the rest of the document is organized.** The Introduction gives the setting, a chronology of the reawakening and the candidate explanations for it. Previous Work follows the literature from White (1964, 1968) to Lindsey and others (2026), the account of the eruption. The next chapter describes the data compiled for this study and compares present chloride and temperature with the historical record, starting with the Lower Terrace. The proxy chapter is the center of the thesis: the questions, hypotheses, equations, methods, the conductivity record so far, the sampling design and the proposed move of two loggers. The schedule and costs follow. The PHREEQC chapter reconstructs the deep fluid, follows it to the springs and the creek, and compares the calculated thermal outflow with earlier estimates. The last chapter covers possible further work (resistivity, a Leapfrog model and surface mapping of the terrace), followed by the expected products and the conclusion. An appendix holds figure slots for the author.

# Introduction

## Study area and setting

Steamboat Hills sits a few kilometers south of Reno, Nevada, at the
northern end of a fault-bounded belt of Great Basin geothermal systems.
Unlike most Great Basin systems, which are amagmatic and derive their heat
from regionally elevated mantle heat flow alone, Steamboat is one of a
small number of magmatic-influenced systems in the province, and it is one
of the longest-studied hydrothermal areas in the western United States,
characterized geologically and hydrologically since the 1950s
[@thompsonwhite1964; @white1964b; @white1968c; @silberman1979]. The field
has produced electricity commercially since the mid-1980s and is currently
operated by Ormat Technologies as a binary, fully reinjected system
generating on the order of 79 MW net [@dhakal2025]. Production and
injection are conventionally divided into three thermal zones (Upper,
Middle, and Lower Steamboat) reflecting a natural-state upflow of roughly
220-240 degrees Celsius beneath Upper Steamboat that cools northeastward
along strike toward the Middle and Lower fields [@dhakal2025;
@johnsonhulen2006].

At the surface, this deep system expresses itself through the Lower Sinter
Terrace, an area of active and historically active fumaroles, seeps, and
hot springs within the Steamboat Springs Area of Critical Environmental
Concern. That surface expression has not been static. Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992] documented a near-total cessation of natural spring flow at
the main and low silica terraces between 1986 and 1989, attributing most
(though not all) of the decline to regional shallow-groundwater drawdown
rather than to geothermal production. Sorey [@sorey2000] revisited the same
terrace roughly a decade later and found that although regional groundwater
levels had by then recovered, natural spring flow at the main terrace had
not resumed. That non-recovery is the single most important piece of
historical context for this proposal: it establishes that surface discharge
at Steamboat is not simply a mirror of groundwater level, and that a system
which goes quiet does not necessarily reawaken on its own.

It was against that backdrop that, beginning around 2022, steaming ground
at the Lower Sinter Terrace began to expand again, and on June 3, 2025, an
uncapped, shallow abandoned well erupted without warning, sending boiling
water roughly 30 meters into the air: the first geyser-like activity
documented at Steamboat in decades [@lindsey2026]. The well was capped in
the following days to weeks, but discharge did not stop; it redistributed
laterally, opening new seeps and spitting vents along nearby fractures.
This event, and the still-open question of what it means for the system's
deeper plumbing, motivates this proposal: a direct re-examination of
Sorey's own chloride-discharge method against the modern system, and a test
of whether continuous conductivity monitoring can substitute for discrete
chloride sampling as a practical way to track that outflow going forward.

## A brief chronology

Three broad periods structure this history, shown in @fig-timeline. The
**historical/characterization period** (roughly 1950-1968) established
the regional geology, structure, and hydrology that every later study,
including this one, still relies on [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1964b;
@white1968c]. The **development period** (1986-2007) covers the
transition from a natural system to a commercially produced one, the
1987-89 spring-flow decline documented by Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], its non-recovery by 2000 [@sorey2000], and the buildout
of the groundwater/geothermal monitor-well network described by
Klein, Johnson, and Spielman [@klein2007]. The **reawakening period**
(2022-present) covers the renewed steaming, the June 2025 eruption,
and this project's own response.

## Candidate explanations for the reactivation

What drove the 2022 to 2025 reactivation is an open question that this proposal does not claim to resolve. Several candidate explanations have some support, and I set them out together so that the injection-permit event on @fig-timeline is not left unexplained. They are not mutually exclusive.

**Increased injection (Ormat).** The one dated regulatory document on file, an NDEP temporary permit [@nevadadep2025uic], raised the field's combined authorized injection limit from 49,500 to 55,000 gpm on 30 May 2025, about two weeks before the first eruption pulse. The timing is suggestive, and @fig-timeline flags it as a candidate and not a confirmed cause. The permit records newly authorized limits, not the rate actually injected, and its reported current pressures sit below the prior ceiling at most wells, so whether injection rose before the eruption or was only newly permitted cannot be settled from this document. Most injection wells were already running at 77 to 90 percent of the maximum flow they can sustain at their allowable pressure (@fig-injpressure; IW-5, IW-6 and 42A-32, for example), which limits how much any single well could add. One well, 23-33, is reported at 135 psig, above its own newly authorized 120 psig, which the permit table states as given.

Where injection happens matters as well as how much. Collar [@collar1990thesis] recorded water-level responses in the Herz 2 and Brown School wells that coincided with injection into OESI well IW-3, and concluded that production wells are better connected to the terrace springs than injection wells. His proposals to inject nearer the terrace aimed at raising head above land surface, which is what spring flow needs. In 1986 to 1989 net production lowered heads, and for 2025 the question is whether injection raised them, since the June 2025 pipe eruption implies heads at that spot stood above land surface. That is a mechanism and a precedent, not evidence of cause. The state permit record for Ormat's 49 Steamboat wells shows continuing drilling and well-status change (injection well 21-32 completed in 2014, 42A-32 in 2018, production well 41-5 in 2012 and now shut in; eight wells are shut in), but it does not show a decline in production. The only repeat production readings are two NDEP tracer-test reports, in which well 24-5 fell from 883 to 835 kph (about 5 percent) over nine months. A new production well, 28A-32, was completed in August 2026, more than a year after the eruption, so it cannot have contributed. Testing this explanation needs dated well-by-well injection and production histories for 2022 to 2025, which I have requested from NDEP and plan to request from Ormat.

```{r fig-injpressure}
  alt = "Two stacked bar charts by injection well: wellhead pressure (historic peak, current, authorized) and injection rate (current versus maximum).",
```

**Conduit reactivation within the existing system.** The 2026 poster [@irvinlindsey2026] found that the fissure's major-ion chemistry and stable isotopes match the fluid already seen in nearby springs and wells, and that paired temperature loggers on the terrace are inversely related (r = -0.68), consistent with discharge shifting between vents in one connected flow system. The near-constant Cl/B ratio across seven decades is independent support. Of the explanations here, this one has the most direct observational support.

**Regional groundwater recovery.** As noted in the Introduction, recovery by 2000 did not restart spring flow [@sorey2000], so recovery alone has not been enough to reactivate the system. Whether a slower, multi-decade continuation crossed a threshold by 2022 is untested.

**Local earthquakes.** White [@white1968c] saw spring responses to six of fifteen earthquakes between 1947 and 1952, all moderate (above about M5) and near. Collar [@collar1990thesis] found no link to the largest event of 1986 to 1989 (M3.9, about 11 miles north). A USGS catalog pull for 2021 to 2026 (M2.5 and above within 60 km) shows four M3.0 to 3.5 events within about 6 km of the field between January and March 2024, when Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] describe the shift from diffuse steaming to discrete seeps and vents. Daily water levels at STMGID MW10, and MW3 from February 2024, show no consistent step at those events (standardized steps from -2.3 to +1.6 across seven comparisons, none robust to the number of tests). A later check against the 2026 temperature and conductance loggers found no conductance steps and only an excess of temperature steps at loggers that already swing with weather. That is consistent with small events having no detectable effect, but two regional wells and a short logger record cannot rule out a local response, so the 2024 cluster is a lead. The largest recent regional events (M4.7 to 4.8 in April 2026) were about 58 km away. Support for this explanation is weak.

**Precipitation and recharge.** A large December 2025 storm raised water level at one regional well and not at a nearby well with a different completion depth. Collar [@collar1990thesis] showed how to test this: 1946 to 1952 spring discharge tracked annual precipitation, the 1949 drought minimum (48 gpm) was far above the 1988 flow (3 to 4 gpm), and a cumulative departure from mean precipitation at Reno and Sky Tavern (1938 to 1989) separated drought from the production signal. The same analysis for Reno Airport (water years 1938 to 2026, mean 187 mm per year, @fig-precipdeparture) shows two dry years just before the 2022 onset (100 and 77 mm in water years 2020 and 2021) that took the cumulative departure to about -220 mm, and a wet 2023 (391 mm) that brought it back to roughly the long-term mean, where it has stayed. The seeps and vents developed during average to wet conditions. The 2022 onset followed a dry spell, but similar and deeper dry spells (2012 to 2015, about -420 mm) are not known to have produced surface activity. This is a descriptive comparison at a station about 15 km north and 100 m lower than the field, not a test.

```{r fig-precipdeparture}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/precip_cumulative_departure.png",
  "Cumulative departure from mean water-year precipitation at Reno Airport, 1938-2026 (NOAA GHCN-Daily USW00023185; complete water years only). The shaded band marks 2022 onset to the June 2025 eruption.",
  alt = "Line chart of cumulative precipitation departure at Reno Airport, 1938-2026, rising from about -220 mm to near zero across a shaded 2022-2025 band.",
  id = "fig-precipdeparture"

```

None of these explanations excludes the others. The calibration and remapping work in the proxy chapter is designed to produce the time-paired chemistry and discharge data that could eventually discriminate between them, and not to settle the question now.

# Previous work

Steamboat is among the most thoroughly studied geothermal systems in the western United States, with published work going back to the 1860s. This chapter goes through that record by what each body of work established, so that the contribution of this proposal is clear against it. It starts with the geologic and structural framework, then the hydrology and the chloride-discharge record that this thesis directly extends. It then covers geochemistry, gas and water quality, the use of conductivity as a solute-flux proxy elsewhere, the reservoir and monitoring-network studies, and finally the 2022 to 2026 reawakening. @tbl-pubtimeline lists the same literature in order of publication, and the chapter closes with what that record leaves open.

## Geologic and structural framework

White, Thompson, and Sandberg [@white1964b; @thompsonwhite1964]
established the geologic framework still used today: a Mesozoic
metamorphic basement intruded by Cretaceous granitic rocks, buried under
more than a hundred cubic miles of mostly andesitic Cenozoic volcanic
rock, and cut by the basin-and-range Steamboat Springs fault zone. White
argued that this fault zone localizes the present thermal area simply
because it is the lowest-elevation fault available for deep thermal water
to intersect the water table, not because it has any special structural
property. His interpretation of the heat source (a large, roughly 50
km^3, slowly cooling magma chamber supplying heat by conduction for at
least 100,000 years, with "no new magma... directly involved" and
volcanic steam contributing under five percent of total system water
[@white1964b]) frames Steamboat as a persistent, long-lived convective
system rather than one newly activated by fresh input, which bears
directly on this proposal's redistribution versus new source question.
Arehart and others [@arehart2003] and Johnson and Hulen [@johnsonhulen2006]
later brought trace-element and gas evidence for a magmatic heat source,
a partly differing view that agrees on the point that matters here: the
heat source is long-lived, not newly arrived. Silberman and others
[@silberman1979] constrained the duration of hydrothermal activity from
spatially associated volcanic rocks.

White's own record also shows that dramatic surface behavior is not new at
Steamboat. He compiled published observations of episodic natural
geysering extending back to 1860-1862 (De Quille, 1876, "the first
published record of geyser observations in the United States"
[@white1968c]) and accounts of drilling-induced eruptions through the
early twentieth century (Lindgren, 1903-1905; Jones, 1912-1914; Gianella,
1939, wells erupting stibnite from depth) [@white1964b]. A 1947-48
Low Terrace well that erupted continuously once drilling intersected its
aquifer is a direct historical analog to the 2025 pipe eruption. The 2025
event is therefore the latest instance of a long-documented pattern, not
an unprecedented one. Vaughan and others [@vaughan2005] later mapped the
surface mineral expression with airborne thermal-infrared imagery,
distinguishing actively forming opaline sinter from older chalcedony
sinter and an acid-sulfate alteration halo around the fumaroles, which
is the kind of surface evidence this proposal's remapping is designed to
update for the post-eruption terrace.

Collar [@collar1990thesis; also Collar and Huntley, @collar1990] contributed the fault and air-photo-
lineament map this thesis treats as its best candidate for the
structural context: it also locates several wells already resolved in
this project's database, which gives natural control points for
digitizing. Skalbeck [@skalbeck2001] supplied the most detailed
geophysical subsurface characterization, interpreting depths to the
principal units (alluvium, volcanic rock, and the altered cap of the
granodiorite bedrock body) along geophysical survey lines, and
tabulating a multi-decade well-monitoring record.

White and others [@white1964b] favor east-dipping normal faults for the Low and Main Terrace structures (the Steamboat Springs fault zone), with a minimum dip of 50 degrees from drill-hole relations. The database carries this as an eastward dip of at least 50 degrees on the seven Main and Low Terrace fault traces, labelled as a zone-level literature value. None of the digitized traces has a measured dip of its own.


Several later studies refine that framework. Silberman and others [@silberman1979] dated volcanic rocks spatially associated with the thermal area and concluded from K-Ar ages that hydrothermal activity has persisted intermittently for at least 2.5 to 3 million years, so the system has a long history of quiet and active periods and not a single onset. Johnson and Hulen [@johnsonhulen2006] proposed a dual control for the northern part of the field: thermal fluid enters wells at shallow depth (less than 350 m) through a low-angle extensional fault zone, and that zone is fed from depth by a Cu-Mo-mineralized, late-Cretaceous magmatic-hydrothermal breccia pipe. They worked from six northern-field wells (34-32, 38-28, 42-32, 44-32, 78-29 and injection well 64A-32), several of which are in this thesis's well network. Arehart and others [@arehart2003] argued from trace elements (arsenic in particular) and gas geochemistry that a magmatic body, and not extensional heat flow alone, supplies heat at Steamboat, which sets it apart from most Great Basin systems and is the reason gas chemistry is treated here as a source-discrimination tool.

Geophysical work gives the subsurface structure. Skalbeck and others [@skalbeck2002] used gravity and aeromagnetic modeling to estimate the volume of the geothermal reservoir. They describe the Steamboat Hills as a northeast-trending bedrock ridge on the western margin of the Basin and Range, cut by north-south, northeast and northwest fault systems, with a line of Pleistocene rhyolite domes along the northeast trend and the geothermal field along the northwest-trending system. Groundwater in the area comes mainly from snowmelt infiltration in the Carson Range and flows east toward Steamboat Creek [@cohenloeltz1964]. Skalbeck's dissertation [@skalbeck2001] extends this with 2.75-D gravity and aeromagnetic modeling along 11 profiles and a Cl/B mixing analysis of alluvial-aquifer and geothermal monitoring wells. It finds that the bulk bedrock and altered volcanic matrix acts as a low-permeability confining layer, while fault zones, some mapped independently by ground magnetics (the Mud Volcano Basin fault, for example), provide the high-conductivity vertical pathways by which thermal water reaches the alluvial aquifer. Huebner and others [@huebner2007] ran gravity, magnetic and resistivity surveys on UNR's Redfield Campus, over the northwest edge of the reservoir. They found a basement offset of about 50 m with a co-located reduction in magnetic susceptibility, consistent with hydrothermal alteration, along a postulated N60E-striking fault that also appears to localize low-flux fumaroles and a phreatic crater. That is a useful analog for the fracture-controlled discharge on the Lower Sinter Terrace, and an example of the geophysical approach proposed in the further-work chapter.

## Hydrology and the chloride-discharge record

This is the body of work the thesis directly extends. White [@white1968c]
measured chloride as a conservative tracer for total system heat flow,
reporting a pre-boiling upflow of 800-820 ppm at about 175 C, and
estimated a roughly 100 gpm thermal inflow to the creek along the Low
Terrace that is not visible at the surface. Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], an administrative report for the Bureau of Land Management,
is the single most detailed historical baseline: it documents the
near-total cessation of natural spring flow at the main and low terraces
between 1986 and 1989 and attributes most, though not all, of it to
regional shallow-groundwater drawdown rather than to production; it
tabulates 1950-1991 chemistry for nine features, a Cl/B ratio near 19 in
1990-91 thermal samples, barometric efficiencies of 0.42-0.45 at two
springs, aquifer-test results, and a chloride mass balance that treats an
820 mg/L thermal and 6 mg/L non-thermal end-member as the two components
of Steamboat Creek flow. Collar's M.S. thesis [@collar1990thesis], written
from the same USGS grant study, applied the same chloride-flux logic to
1988-89 discharge measurements, 35 years before this proposal's version of
it, and is treated in detail below. Sorey and Spielman [@sorey2008; @sorey2017]
refined the chloride mass balance method at two Steamboat Creek gauging
sites, Rhodes Road (SBRR) and Bella Vista (SBBV), reporting 730-1,214
gallons per minute for 2007-08 and an average of 60 liters per second
(range 45-90 L/s) across 24 sampling events from 2008 to 2016. Cohen and
Loeltz [@cohenloeltz1964] characterized Truckee Meadows groundwater
outside the field, providing background for several wells this proposal
uses for its barometric-efficiency calculation.

Collar's thesis [@collar1990thesis] is the most complete single treatment of
the 1986-89 decline and the closest methodological predecessor of this
proposal. Over 1986-89 he logged water levels in about a dozen main- and
low-terrace spring vents, strat and observation wells, and private alluvial
wells, gaged Steamboat Creek, Galena Creek, and the ditches at 63 stations in
three surveys (June-July 1988, August 1988, March 1989), and tested earthquakes, barometric pressure, earth tides,
precipitation, a nearby spa well, and geothermal production as candidate
causes. He concluded that discharging wells in the CPI field, and to a much
lesser degree the OESI field, were the principal cause of the decline, on the
grounds that spring levels fell during production and recovered during
shut-ins, many springs moved in parallel, spring hydrographs mimicked those of
observation wells known to be connected to the production wells, and natural
thermal discharge to the creek had fallen. Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992],
working on the same period and drawing on overlapping data, reached a
different weighting: 80-95 percent of the roughly 17 ft head decline beneath
the main terrace attributed to shallow South Truckee Meadows groundwater
decline and only 1-3 ft (5-20 percent) to the CPI field. The two analyses
agree on the facts that matter most for this proposal: the CPI field is
hydraulically connected to strat wells 2 and 9, heads beneath the terrace
fell by about 17 ft, and drought alone does not explain the decline. They
disagree on how much of the head loss was caused by production, which is
exactly the kind of attribution question that a pressure or injection
change would raise again, and it remains unresolved.

Collar's creek work uses the same two end-member chloride balance as this
proposal (thermal water 820 mg/L, nonthermal 4 mg/L), with explicit
equations for gaining and losing reaches, and divides the creek at Virginia
City Highway (Geiger Grade) into a "geothermal area" reach and a South
Truckee Meadows reach extending to Huffaker Hills. His June 1988 and March
1989 surveys put thermal inflow to the creek at 490-530 and 660 gpm,
about 60 to 80 percent of White's 1955 value, with the shortfall concentrated
near the main and low terraces (about 60 percent of 1955) rather than
downstream (about 80 percent). He also records that Shump's earlier estimate
[@shump1985], made with specific conductivity, changed substantially when its
nonthermal end-member was set consistently with White's chloride value,
because specific conductivity and chloride are not directly related in the
carbonate- and bicarbonate-dominated nonthermal groundwater of the South
Truckee Meadows. That is a documented precedent for the failure mode this
proposal's conductance-proxy test is designed to detect. Two further results
bear directly on the Lower Sinter Terrace. First, during 1989 an intermittently
pumped well at the Steamboat Spa, about 2,800 ft south of the main terrace,
produced weekday drawdown spikes and weekend recoveries in well GS-1 and the
old spa well on the low terrace and lowered spring 50, while main-terrace
springs 6 and 12 did not respond, so the low terrace is hydraulically
sensitive to nearby withdrawal in a way the main terrace is not. Second, of
twenty low-terrace springs White cataloged (nine of them geysers), only spring
50 was still flowing (about 3 gpm) in 1988, and spring 50 was the one spring
where Nehring found young meteoric water mixing with thermal water in 1977.

@fig-discharge puts the published estimates and this project's own 2026 value on one time axis, with the basis of each (creek inflow, or creek inflow plus wells) labeled, because the 1950s and 1960s figures were not all measured the same way.

```{r fig-discharge}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/discharge_through_time.png",
  "Thermal-water discharge to Steamboat Creek, 1955-2026, creek-inflow basis except where labeled. White's 1955 point excludes wells; the 1964 point includes them; Shump's is specific-conductivity based; reaches differ slightly between studies.",
  alt = "Line and point plot of estimated thermal-water discharge to Steamboat Creek from 1955 to 2026.",
  id = "fig-discharge"
)
```

Two earlier studies add geochemical constraints on the thermal fluid. Nehring [@nehring1979] used enthalpy-chloride and deuterium-chloride diagrams, chemical geothermometers and bicarbonate to chloride ratios on 1977 spring samples to estimate a deep thermal fluid of about 700 mg/L chloride and a deuterium value near -117 per mil, and found about 10 percent cold-water mixing at spring 50 and at two wells on the Herz property. His longer open-file report [@nehring1980] gives the 1977 sampling, the analyses, the silica, Na-K and Na-K-Ca geothermometers and the mixing models in full, and reproduces White's well data. Regional context for the cold end-member of every chloride balance comes from Cohen and Loeltz [@cohenloeltz1964], whose study of Truckee Meadows hydrogeology and hydrogeochemistry describes the recharge and flow directions of the groundwater that mixes with the thermal water.

## Geochemistry, gas, and water quality

Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995] built the most useful modern geochemical dataset for the field. They report major-ion and gas data and geothermometry for two well fields, a high-temperature field (the Caithness wells, including 23-5) and a moderate-temperature field (Far West, with the PW2-x and PW3-x wells), and a conceptual model in which deep fluid of 230 to 235 C rising near well 23-5 boils to feed the moderate-temperature field and the sinter-terrace hot springs. Their D'Amore and Panichi gas-geothermometer data are the validation set for the gas calculations in this thesis, which reproduce their published temperatures for well 23-5 to within 0.3 C. Two shorter U.S. Geological Survey project reports bracket that paper. Janik and Mariner [@janikmariner1994] describe the first sampling campaign in November 1991 and report a deep reservoir fluid of about 750 mg/L chloride, and Mariner and Janik [@mariner1996] place Steamboat in a comparative survey of granitic-rock-hosted systems that also includes Coso and Roosevelt Hot Springs.

Statewide geochemical studies give context for interpreting those data. Shevenell and De Rocher [@shevenell2005] benchmarked silica, Na-K-Ca and multicomponent geothermometers against measured production temperatures at Nevada power plants, including Steamboat wells 28-33, 41-33A and 23-5 (reservoir temperatures of 150 to 247 C). They concluded that no single geothermometer is reliable alone and that comparing several is itself diagnostic, which supports the multi-method approach used in the PHREEQC chapter. Shevenell and others [@shevenell2002] began a statewide program of sampling thermal and nonthermal waters (major and trace elements, stable isotopes and noble gases) and list Steamboat among the few Nevada sites with existing noble-gas data. A later field method from the same group, soil-CO2 flux surveys [@shevenell2014], found no thermal anomaly at an active hot-spring discharge site but anomalous fluxes above two boiling thermal-gradient wells at a separate blind system. The method transfers to the Lower Sinter Terrace, though it has not been applied there.

Two studies address water quality in Steamboat Creek itself and bear on how much of the creek's conductance is not thermal. Lyons and others [@lyons1998] measured total mercury in the creek and found concentrations 40 to 60 times those of pristine mountain streams, and discuss the contributions of natural geothermal input and of anthropogenic, mining-related sources. Romeis and others [@romeis2002] used three 1998 water-quality surveys and a calibrated WASP5 model to attribute nonpoint nitrate loading in upper Steamboat Creek mainly to septic systems in two residential reaches (Pleasant Valley and Steamboat Valley). Both are reminders that conductance at an upstream or downstream station can reflect inputs other than thermal water, which is part of what the calibration here has to separate.

## Conductivity as a solute-flux proxy elsewhere

The idea of replacing discrete chloride samples with a continuous conductivity record has strong precedent. McCleskey and others [@mccleskey2012] showed that chloride and other geothermal solutes (sodium, sulfate, fluoride, bicarbonate, silica, potassium, lithium, boron and arsenic) correlate linearly with electrical conductivity (R-squared above 0.9) in the Madison, Firehole and Gibbon Rivers of Yellowstone, so that continuous conductivity could replace much more labor-intensive sampling for solute flux. A follow-up extended the approach to the Snake River and, through a synoptic tributary study, identified the Lewis River as the dominant source (50 to 80 percent) of several conservative solutes [@mccleskey2016], a design much like the paired upstream and downstream loggers used here. Two papers from other systems offer method and not data. Newman and Pepin [@newman2026] rank the susceptibility of springs at Steamboat Springs, Colorado (a different low-temperature system that shares only the name) using water-temperature variance, tritium and carbon-14 residence times, and a stream mass balance that put more than 80 percent of discharge in diffuse and small springs. Janik and others [@janik2000] document Anderson Springs in the vapor-dominated SE Geysers field and weigh a 1889 to 1999 series of abrupt spring temperature and chemistry changes against competing explanations (reservoir depletion versus seismically enhanced fracture flow), a good model for how a long chloride record should be argued. They also state the accuracy of their digitized fault traces (0.8 km), a precedent for stating the accuracy of this thesis's own fault digitizing.

## Reservoir, monitoring-network, and operator-scale work

Reservoir-scale work places the surface focus of this thesis in the operator's larger picture. Combs and Goranson [@combs1994] drilled three slim holes in 1991 (262 to 277 m deep, bottom-hole temperatures 163 to 166 C), found very high fracture permeability in the granodiorite (no pressure rise during an 11 kg/s injection test), and give the fullest published account of the field's development from the 1920s to the SB#2 and SB#3 plants of 1990 to 1993. Goranson [@goranson1995] characterized injection wells IW-1, IW-4 and IW-5 (825, 550 and 330 m deep) with pressure-temperature-spinner logs in 1992, and Goranson and Combs [@goranson2000] used the slim holes plus two more (GTH 87-29 and MTH 21-33) to monitor water level and temperature for years. They found levels fell from 1992 to spring 1996 and then rebounded with Carson Range precipitation and Steamboat Creek discharge, a link between deep water levels and the surface record that is a precedent for the comparisons made here.

Klein and others [@klein2007] documented the groundwater and geothermal monitor-well network: a phreatic aquifer that flows down into the reservoir except in extreme drawdown, an 11,000-record database across 197 wells and springs, and Ormat's planned tracer test and monitor-well redesign after the casing failure of injection well Cox I-1 and a leak at 64A-32. Their Figure 1 is the well-identity map that much of this thesis's site resolution rests on. Bjornsson and others [@bjornsson2014] built a 3-D iTOUGH2 model calibrated to more than 130 wells and 1,270 datasets, which shows a deep recharge of 95 kg/s at 236 to 250 C and a natural-state convective cell with a temperature reversal at 900 to 1,100 m depth beneath the center and north of the wellfield. Dhakal and others [@dhakal2025] updated the numerical model after forty years of production and give the conceptual model used throughout this thesis: a natural-state upflow of 220 to 240 C beneath Upper Steamboat, cooling along northeast-striking faults to 184 C and 168 C in Middle and Lower Steamboat, with a development history from 1920s direct use through the first four power plants (1986 to 1993) and Ormat's 2004 consolidation to a fully reinjected binary system of 79 MW net in 2024. Akerley and others [@akerley2021] describe the directional well 83C-6ST1, the only non-vertical well survey available here. State and federal agency records (the Nevada Divisions of Environmental Protection, Minerals and Water Resources, and the U.S. Geological Survey) supply the chemistry, permit, well-construction and streamflow records that carry this baseline into the present.

## The 2022-2026 reawakening

Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] published the first full account of
the 2022-2025 reawakening and the June 2025 eruption, tracing the stages
from renewed diffuse steaming to discrete seeps and vents to the
eruption itself, and documenting that capping the well did not stop
discharge but redistributed it laterally. This project's own preliminary
chloride-discharge estimate following the eruption, co-authored with
Lindsey, was presented as a poster at the 2026 Geothermal Rising
Conference in Houston, Texas [@irvinlindsey2026]. It found major-ion and
isotope chemistry at the fissure matching nearby springs and wells, an
inverse correlation between paired terrace temperature loggers
(r = -0.68), and a thermal inflow of about 27 L/s against the 2008-2016
average of 60 L/s, and it concluded that the evidence favored
redistribution within an existing conduit network over a new source.
This proposal turns that one-time estimate into a repeatable,
database-grounded one and tests the conclusion against more data.

The same account carries the thermal-infrared work that this proposal builds on.
Lindsey and others flew visible-light and thermal drones over the same 67 acres
of the terrace and creek in July and October 2025, with persistent
GPS-surveyed ground-control points, and tuned the thermograms against six
high-emissivity ground-control targets [@lindsey2026]. The calibrated mosaics
agree with the target temperatures to within 1.3 degrees Celsius (1.0 for the
low-altitude flight), although a small near-boiling vent reads only 59-78
degrees Celsius against 80-90 measured, because a centimeter-scale source is
averaged across a 7 cm pixel, and creek water reads several degrees warmer in
the mosaics than in the loggers. The surveys identified steaming fissures
at the eruptive area, warm ground and springs near Steamboat Hot Springs
Resort, and warm seeps and hot springs along both banks of Steamboat Creek,
including previously unmarked springs on the east bank (about 60 degrees
Celsius, confirmed in the field). Differencing the two flights showed a large
area of warm ground near the resort up to 15 degrees Celsius cooler in
October than in July. That calibration is what allows this proposal to treat
the imagery quantitatively; the subsection "The thermal layer and the
database on one map" below measures it against the project's own points.

**What this body of work leaves open.** The record is rich on geology, reservoir behavior and the chloride-flux method, and it stops short of the question this thesis asks. Chloride discharge has been measured only from campaigns of discrete samples, so no one has seen how thermal outflow varies from day to day or season to season, and none of the work tested whether a continuous proxy could stand in for those samples at this site. The 1986 to 1989 decline was studied in detail, but the 2022 to 2025 reactivation has only one full account [@lindsey2026] and a poster. The geochemical studies describe the deep fluid and the wells and springs of the field, but not how that fluid changes between the fissure and the creek, or how the creek chemistry should respond when the source changes. And conductance has been shown to track chloride in Yellowstone rivers but not yet in a smaller, ditch-influenced creek with cold, carbonate-rich non-thermal water, where the earlier conductivity-based estimate of Shump had to be revised. This thesis addresses those gaps with a calibrated conductance proxy, a defensible sampling design, and a geochemical account of the fluid from fissure to creek.

# The data compiled for this study {#sec-data}

The first part of the work was to bring the existing record for this system into one place, because the data are scattered across agencies, decades and formats. Chemistry from the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP), including the public-records request for the Ormat plant outlets, sits next to my own field samples, the loggers, USGS discharge, weather and pressure records, well logs and permits, and chemistry transcribed from the older papers (Sorey and Colvard, Mariner and Janik, Skalbeck, Collar). Each source arrives with different site names, units and detection limits, so most of the effort went into harmonizing them: one location table with aliases for the old names, one set of analyte codes, and conversions to common units. This chapter shows what that bought. It lays out the monitoring network, then compares present chloride and temperature with the historical record at the same wells and springs, starting with the Lower Sinter Terrace and then the wider network, and finishes with the thermal map of the terrace.


## Monitoring network and supporting database

The database is the backbone of the project. It holds my field sampling at the Lower Sinter Terrace; state chemistry, permit, well-construction and water-rights records; federal streamflow, water-level, weather and historical conductance records; and chemistry I transcribed by hand from the older papers (Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992], Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995], and Skalbeck [@skalbeck2001]). It currently holds about 1,650 samples from about 380 wells plus springs, seeps and creek sites. Keeping everything in one place means a question that spans several decades and agencies is answered the same way each time, instead of being rebuilt from spreadsheets. Checks run on every update for missing values, implausible readings and internal consistency. One of them mattered for the results below: a missing alkalinity parameter in one chemistry feed made the charge-balance error look like about 60 percent. After the fix the median error is 0.7 percent, and most samples pass the usual 5 percent threshold.

@tbl-datasources lists each source used in this thesis, what it measures, its resolution and period, the amount on file, and the role it plays. The continuous records are the two conductivity loggers and the temperature loggers, together with the USGS gauges; everything else is a discrete sample, a reading or a mapped feature. The imagery and elevation data set the spatial resolution of the maps in this document.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\footnotesize
```

**Well and borehole records.** The same drill hole often shows up under different names, coordinates and depths in different sources, so each source gets its own entry in the database, and lists of wells are kept in a staging table that records how every row was matched. A value on file is changed only when a primary source gives a different one. The USGS test holes of White and others [@white1964b; @white1968c] show how this works. A 2019 state compilation put hole GS-6 about 1.6 km east of its position on White's map. The elevation model agrees with White's stated altitude at the map position and not at the compilation's, so the map position is used. Skalbeck's well table [@skalbeck2001] agrees with White for GS-5 but gives GS-7 an altitude about 90 m too high and GS-6 a depth of 289 m against White's 65 m, so the database uses White's values and keeps Skalbeck's GS-6 as a separate, unconfirmed well. A 2009 state list of 145 wells and a 2019 compilation were matched row by row against the wells already loaded. About 800 m is the best position known for the 30 new wells indexed from state logs east of the terraces, so wells that uncertain are kept out of the three-dimensional collar table.


**Spring and well remapping.** Several springs on the Lower Sinter Terrace are listed as inactive in the operator's records. A central field task is to walk the terrace and confirm for each one whether it is dry, seeping or flowing. So far this has produced 51 GPS-tagged points: 28 seeps, 13 areas of steaming ground, 7 springs and 3 creek points.

**Chemistry and isotope sampling.** I collect water at springs, wells and creek stations and measure pH, temperature and specific conductance on site. The laboratory then runs major ions, alkalinity, trace elements and oxygen and hydrogen isotopes. My own campaign has collected 71 samples so far.

**Temperature logger network.** Eleven temperature loggers sit at springs, wells and along the fissure. They give a continuous record of whether the thermal signature at the eruption site is steady, cooling or moving since the wellhead was capped.


@fig-fissure-series shows chloride and Cl/B in the geothermal source itself, the fissure area and the other thermal wells and springs sampled since 1950. These samples are not part of the creek calibration. The fissure area is separated from the creek in space, and probably in time, because the outflow travel time is unknown, so the series shows how the source changes and not what the creek will do. The 2025 and 2026 fissure-area values (chloride 470 to 915 mg/L, Cl/B 19 to 23) sit within the range of the thermal samples since 1950, which is consistent with a source that has changed little in chloride and Cl/B over the period, with few samples and different laboratories.

```{r fig-fissure-series}
  alt = "Two dot plots of chloride and Cl/B through time, fissure-area samples in orange clustered at 2025 to 2026 and older thermal samples in blue.",
  id = "fig-fissure-series"

```

@fig-temp-context shows the temperature loggers with barometric pressure, precipitation and earthquakes on one date axis. The loggers hold the data from April to September 2026 (plus an earlier record at SBS_0006), and the context series run to November 2026. No cause is tested in the figure. It is the visual check of which events fall inside the logger record: the largest storm of the winter and the nearest earthquakes both fall before most loggers were deployed.

```{r fig-temp-context}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/temperature_context_timeseries.png",
  "Hourly temperature at the loggers (top two panels), with daily Reno sea-level pressure, daily precipitation and earthquakes (distance to the field, size by magnitude) below, October 2025 to November 2026.",
  alt = "Stacked time series: logger temperatures, barometric pressure, precipitation bars and earthquake distances.",
  id = "fig-temp-context"
)
```

**Do earthquakes line up with changes at the loggers?** Each earthquake in the logger record was compared with the 48 hours before and after at every temperature and conductance logger, and the difference was scored against that logger's normal 48-hour changes (z score). No conductance step exceeded 2 in 38 comparisons (about 2 would be expected by chance). The temperature loggers show more: 19 of 215 comparisons exceeded 2 in size where about 10 would be expected by chance, almost all for earthquakes 15 to 60 km away, and the largest steps are at the fumarole and spring loggers (A004 SBS_0003, A010 SBS_0006, A005 SBF_0001) whose temperatures already swing with weather and the daily cycle. Only 2 comparisons involve an earthquake within 15 km. This is an excess of about two times chance, with overlapping windows and no control for weather, so it is a lead to follow with the next download and not evidence of a response. The nearest and largest events (M2 to 3) are small, and the new Reno-area download added no events that were not already in the catalog.


@tbl-fieldtogis summarizes how this project's field mapping and the
historically documented wells and springs all flow through the same
database into the same GIS export, a single traceable path from a GPS point
in the field to a layer a committee member could open in ArcGIS.

```{r tbl-fieldtogis}
field_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/monitoring_network/fieldwork_to_database_to_gis_summary.csv")
names(field_tbl) <- c("Source", "N", "Detail", "Database tables", "In GIS export?")
field_tbl[["Database tables"]] <- gsub("_", " ", gsub("/", ", ", field_tbl[["Database tables"]]))
field_tbl[["In GIS export?"]] <- gsub("_", " ", field_tbl[["In GIS export?"]])
knitr::kable(
  field_tbl, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "c", "l", "l", "l"),
  caption = "Field mapping and historically documented locations, traced from source through this project's database to the GeoPackage GIS export."
)
```

## Seasonal variation: the regional monitoring network compared to the Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath

The monitoring network has construction detail (completion interval, elevation, total depth) that the Lower Sinter Terrace samples do not, as @tbl-wellconstruction shows. SBF_0001, SBW_0001, SBW_0002 and the three springs and seep have no well record at all, while STMGID MW3 and MW10 and several of the monitoring wells sampled in the 2025 rounds do. One unit problem is flagged and not silently fixed: Herz Domestic Well's completion interval (12 to 34) is stored in meters, left over from the Skalbeck data, while every other well in the table is in feet. Units need checking before completion depths are compared across sources.

```{r tbl-wellconstruction}
well_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/monitoring_network/monitoring_well_construction_summary.csv")
knitr::kable(
  well_tbl, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Well", "Elevation (m)", "Total depth", "Top perforation", "Bottom perforation"),
  caption = "Construction data on file for the regional monitoring network. Units are feet except Herz Domestic Well's completion interval (meters, flagged in text)."
)
```

Field-parameter rounds at the eight monitoring and domestic wells and the injection-side outlets, from August to December 2025 (@fig-fieldchem), show how much conductance, pH and temperature move from month to month away from the terrace. Some outlets swing by more than 1,500 microsiemens per centimeter across the rounds, while the shallow domestic wells stay fairly flat. Water levels tell a similar story (@fig-wlstandardized). After standardizing each well's depth to water against its own mean and spread, Herz Domestic Well tracks STMGID MW3 closely (r about 0.94, p about 0.005, n = 6) but not MW10 (r about -0.57, not significant). That fits MW3's short, shallow screen (100 feet, at 186 to 286 feet) sharing more of a shallow signal with Herz Domestic than MW10's 480-foot, deeper screen does.

For comparison, the conductivity loggers on the creek (@fig-conductivity-timeseries) cover a different window, July to October 2026, so this is not a same-time comparison. They show a fairly small swing, about 330 to 370 microsiemens per centimeter at SBRR and 1,040 to 1,130 at SBGG, while some regional wells swing by a factor of two or more over their own rounds. Taken with the construction-data gap above, the regional network already shows well-to-well seasonal variability large enough to matter for any flowpath comparison. The flowpath wells and springs still need construction data and an overlapping seasonal record before the comparison can be made directly.

## Historical comparison: chloride and temperature at previously documented wells and springs

The same stability question can be asked of individual wells and springs, not just the pooled thermal end-member. Seventeen sites have independently sourced chloride records. Twelve span more than one sampling campaign (Sorey and Colvard [-@sorey1992], Mariner and Janik [-@mariner1995], Skalbeck's [-@skalbeck2001] 1985 to 1998 monthly monitoring, and NDEP), and five have only the 2024 NDEP public-records samples. @fig-histcl and @fig-histtemp show them side by side.

```{r fig-histcl}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/historical_cl_by_well.png",
  "Chloride through time at seventeen historically documented wells and springs, every measurement on file. The bottom five panels (Boyd Domestic, Eich, Jeppson Geothermal, Rogers Domestic, Soccer Field) hold two 2024 NDEP Public Records Request samples each; panels use independent y-axes.",
  alt = "Seventeen-panel scatter and line plot of chloride over time, one panel per well or spring, with sparse 2024 points at five wells.",
  id = "fig-histcl"
)
```

```{r fig-histtemp}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/historical_temperature_by_well.png",
  "Temperature through time at the same sites, every field-measured value on file (sites with no field temperature record have no panel data).",
  alt = "Multi-panel scatter and line plot of field-measured temperature over time, one panel per well or spring.",
  id = "fig-histtemp"
)
```

The pattern is neither steady decline nor steady stability. Several wells (Herz Domestic, Brown's School, Flame and Pine Tree Ranch-1) show chloride and temperature rising together through the late 1980s and early 1990s. Herz Domestic and Brown's School then decline again by the late 1990s. That differs from the near-constant Cl/B ratio of the thermal end-member over the same decades. Wells on the margin of the thermal field can swing a lot in absolute thermal signature over several years while the deep source's conservative ratios stay fixed, which fits these wells sampling a variable mixing zone and not the source. Steinhardt shows the opposite, falling from 300 to about 140 mg/L between 1987 and 1990, while GS-5, 23-5 and Cox I-1, closer to the historic core of the field, stay high and stable over shorter records.

The five NDEP public-records wells give the only present-day anchors in the figure, with two samples each (March and June 2024). Eich (530 to 590 mg/L) and Soccer Field (470 to 570) carry a clear thermal chloride signature, Boyd (39 to 45) is dilute, and Jeppson (11) and Rogers (7) look like background. Two samples four months apart cannot show a trend, so these points place each well on the thermal to dilute spectrum today and do not test drift. NDOT and Herz Deep were sampled for field parameters in 2025 but have no laboratory chloride on file and are not plotted. The NDEP data request is meant to close that gap.

None of the seventeen sites is on the Lower Sinter Terrace. The springs and seep my fieldwork has confirmed there (SBS_0001, SBS_0002, SBS_0003) and the new hot spring found in August 2026 have nothing like this baseline, because they are known from one field season. That is an argument for the ongoing remapping and the sampling plan in the proxy chapter. Without a comparable multi-year record on the terrace, there is no way yet to tell whether its springs rise and fall like several of these wells or track the apparent stability of the thermal end-member. The monitoring plan is set up to answer that question.

## Surface thermal imaging: what a thermogram can and cannot measure

A thermal camera records infrared radiance, which is converted to surface temperature using the emissivity of the target. Water, wet ground and rock have emissivities near 0.95, so a calibrated thermogram is a good measure of the temperature of the skin of the surface and a poor measure of the temperature just below it. Lindsey and others [@lindsey2026] tune their thermograms against high-emissivity ground-control targets and report agreement within 1.3 degrees Celsius, but they also show where the method fails: a centimeter-scale vent near boiling reads 59-78 degrees Celsius because it is averaged across a 7 cm pixel, creek water reads several degrees warm, and ground a few centimeters down is warmer than the surface. Flights before dawn limit solar heating, which matters here because a sunlit road or roof can reach 30 degrees Celsius with no geothermal input at all.

Two consequences shape how the imagery is used in this thesis. First, the temperature ramp of the map used here ends at 44 degrees Celsius, so the hottest vents are recorded only as "at least 44" and areas above 30 degrees Celsius are a lower bound on how much ground is warm. Second, the area of warm surface is not the same as discharge. A small, hot vent and a broad, slightly warm seepage face can carry the same flow, and a hot tank surface says nothing about how much water passed through it. The surface temperature can be turned into a rough heat loss to the air (convection plus radiation, which is several hundred watts per square meter for ground 30 degrees warmer than the air), and that heat can be compared with the heat carried by the water, but only as an order of magnitude check.

## The thermal layer and the database on one map

**Data and method.** The thermal map used here is a georeferenced layout export
of the 2025 survey (O. Callahan, NBMG, unpublished imagery), in NAD83 / UTM zone 11N
(EPSG:26911), 16,907 by 4,477 pixels at about 0.17 by 0.10 m. A semi-transparent
temperature layer lies over a hillshade, with analyst annotations (yellow ellipses
and 13.5 m circles, outlines) drawn into the pixels. Each pixel was matched to the
nearest color of the 7-44 degree Celsius ramp in the calibrated legend (the TIFF has
no legend of its own, so the same stretch is assumed), keeping pixels within a fixed
color distance of the ramp and excluding the annotation colors. The mask was closed
over about 0.5 m, because the layer is speckled at pixel scale, and polygonized into
a table of thermal areas in the project database. The ramp saturates at 44 degrees Celsius.

**How much surface is hot.** A pixel by pixel count gives 488 m^2^ at or above 30
degrees Celsius; the 67 polygons total 480 m^2^ (@tbl-thermalareas). Grouped by the source
each polygon marks (@tbl-thermalsources and @fig-thermalsources), the Lower Terrace channel
holds the most (161 m^2^, 34 percent), followed by the resort tanks, pipe and pavement
(109 m^2^, 23 percent), the fissure zone (99 m^2^, 21 percent) and the creek-corridor springs
and seeps (49 m^2^, 10 percent, spread over 17 small polygons along the creek). A 13 m^2^
streak at the end of the resort pipe line is uncertain, and the annotated 13.5 m circles
(34 m^2^) are ambiguous. The annotation ellipses are an analyst's judgment, not a verified
geothermal boundary, and a pixel at 30 degrees Celsius is not necessarily geothermal.

**Alignment with mapped structure.** In @fig-map-fissure, about 35 percent of the hot area lies within 5 m of a mapped fissure and 61 percent within 15 m, and 42 percent lies within 15 m of a mapped fault. The streak follows the Low Terrace Fault, and the resort tanks sit about 8 m from it, which would fit the observation that discharge from the spa wells affected springs on the low terrace [@collar1990thesis; @sorey1992]. **Checking my own points against the layer.** Overlaying the points showed that the stored position of SBF_0001 was about 50 m from the hot streak although its logger read up to 88 degrees Celsius, and that SBW_0003 (the capped eruption pipe) had only a provisional position. I replaced them with positions placed in ArcGIS on the imagery: SBF_0001 (moved about 50 m), SBF_0002 (4 m), SBW_0003 (61 m), SBS_0002 (141 m) and SBO_00006 (3 m). The fumarole and pipe points and the NV26-1 gas sample now fall within 0.2 to 3.4 m of a hot pixel and about 1 m of Fissure 42. SBS_0003 sits where the surface shows no thermal anomaly, and SBS_0004, destroyed, is off the thermal map. Nine of the project's points lie within 10 m of a White or Collar feature and carry that name as an alias (the SBF_0001 and SBF_0002 fumaroles as "25ss" and "spring 25ss", SBO_00017 and SBO_00018 as spring 45, SBO_00020 as spring 46, SBO_00015 as spring 44e and SBO_00011 as spring 50n). Those matches rest on proximity and not on a field-confirmed identity.

**The resort's contribution.** The A009 logger sits 7 m from the bright tank pads, so the pads are the resort tanks (@fig-map-resort). Resort infrastructure accounts for 109 m^2^ (23 percent) of the area at or above 30 degrees Celsius. No continuous path at or above 20 degrees Celsius connects the tanks to the creek, so the route of the resort discharge is not mapped, and a field walk of the overflow is planned. On 1 May 2026 the creek chloride fluxes between SBRR and SBBV imply 58.65 L/s of thermal inflow, and any resort water reaching the creek between the two stations is counted in it. At the historical spa-well rates, the resort's share of that inflow would be roughly 2 to 18 percent. The share table, the tank logger's daily schedule and the heat budget are in Appendix A.

**What the thermal layer cannot show.** The imagery was tuned to ground-control targets by Lindsey and others, but I have not independently checked the exported TIFF against logger data, because no logger record overlaps the flight windows and loggers sit in water or fumaroles while the camera sees the surface skin. Where the TIFF has data at a logger it reads far below the logger (the resort tank about 43 C, at the ramp's cap, against 62 to 66 C in July), as expected for a surface measurement with a 44 degree ceiling. The flight date of the TIFF is not recorded, the polygons are the area of hot surface and not of discharge, and the ellipse and circle annotations are an analyst's choices. The GeoPackage export carries the polygons and the alias groupings so that all of this can be checked against the imagery in ArcGIS.

# The chloride-conductance proxy {#sec-proxy}

This chapter is the core of the thesis. Chloride is the standard tracer for thermal water in Steamboat Creek, but it takes a laboratory sample to measure, so the discharge of thermal water has been estimated only a few times in seventy years. Specific conductance can be logged every few minutes for almost nothing. If conductance tracks chloride closely enough, a logger gives a continuous record of thermal outflow, and the 2025 eruption becomes the first event at Steamboat whose aftermath can be followed that closely. The chapter sets out the research questions and hypotheses, the equations, the methods, what the two loggers have recorded so far, how often samples need to be taken, and what the work is expected to cost. It ends with a refinement to the logger locations that came out of the 2026 record.


## Chloride discharge as a tracer of geothermal outflow

Michael Sorey's work on this system [@sorey1992; @sorey2008; @sorey2017] is the starting point for the thesis. Chloride is neither added nor removed by mineral reactions or degassing on the way to discharge, so the difference in chloride mass flux between two points on Steamboat Creek gives the thermal water entering the creek between them, without having to find and measure every spring and seep. Sorey and Spielman applied this at two stations, Rhodes Road (SBRR) and Bella Vista (SBBV), and reported 730 to 1,214 gallons per minute for 2007 to 2008 [@sorey2008] and an average of 60 liters per second (range 45 to 90) over 24 sampling events from 2008 to 2016 [@sorey2017].

The 2026 poster I wrote with Cary Lindsey used the same method and stations to ask whether the 2025 eruption activated a new geothermal source or redistributed fluid within an existing conduit network [@irvinlindsey2026]. It favored redistribution on two grounds. Major-ion chemistry and stable isotopes showed the reactivated fissure discharging the same fluid already seen in nearby springs and wells, and paired temperature loggers on the terrace were inversely related (r = -0.68), as if discharge were shifting between vents within one connected, shallow, fracture-controlled system. The poster's chloride flux put post-eruption thermal inflow at about 27 L/s, below the 2008 to 2016 average of 60 L/s, so overall discharge may have fallen even as flow paths reorganized. This thesis turns that one-time calculation into a repeatable one and asks the question again with more data.

The weakness of the chloride-flux method is that it needs laboratory samples at a frequency most field campaigns cannot sustain. The central contribution of the thesis is to test whether continuous specific conductance, already used as a chloride proxy for geothermal solute flux in Yellowstone's rivers [@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016], can do the same job at Steamboat, so that a sparse set of chloride samples can be calibrated against a continuous conductance record. Studies of discharge-point chemistry at other geothermal systems, such as the low-temperature springs of Steamboat Springs, Colorado (a different system that shares only a name) [@newman2026] and Anderson Springs in the Geysers field [@janik2000], offer methods and not data for this site.

## Purpose of study

**How the study is scoped.** The work starts at the fissure, the most visible and best-documented expression of the 2025 eruption, where I hold a paired water and gas sample, a temperature-logger record and photographs. It then widens in steps: to the other features of the Lower Sinter Terrace (the resort-tank well, three springs and seeps, and the new hot spring found in August 2026), to ask whether they share the fissure's deep source; to Steamboat Creek, where the SBRR and SBGG loggers and the chloride balance combine the thermal discharge of the whole terrace into one signal; and finally to the regional network of production, injection, monitoring and domestic wells, which gives the historical baseline. Each step uses the same tools, so a result at the fissure can be checked at the creek and across the network.

**Central question.** Can continuous conductivity measurements be used to estimate chloride discharge and geothermal outflow at Steamboat Hills, and what do they show about the evolution of the hydrothermal system after the 2025 eruption?

Four research questions follow, each with a deliverable.

**RQ1: How stable is the chloride-conductivity relationship through time and across site types?** Does one calibration apply everywhere, or do outlet, creek, well and spring waters each need their own, and how much uncertainty comes from seasonal variation? *Deliverable:* one or more calibration equations with stated uncertainty.

**RQ2: What is the minimum chloride-sampling frequency that keeps a conductivity-based flux estimate defensible?** *Deliverable:* a monitoring-design recommendation from the Monte Carlo analysis below.

**RQ3: Is conductance driven mainly by conservative mixing, or by reactions that decouple it from chloride?** Is chloride itself conservative here, and are mineral reactions changing conductance independently of it? *Deliverable:* a PHREEQC-based justification for the proxy, or a documented limitation.

**RQ4: Has geothermal outflow changed since the 2025 eruption?** *Deliverable:* a post-eruption reading of chloride flux, conservative-tracer ratios and outlet chemistry against the 70-year discharge record of Sorey and others.

**Working hypotheses.** For RQ1, one calibration will not fit every site type equally well, because outlet, creek, well and spring waters see different near-surface conditions, but the relation should hold within a site type. For RQ2, daily to weekly chloride sampling should keep the estimate defensible, and the open question is where it breaks down. For RQ3, chloride should be conservative everywhere, while conductance will decouple from it wherever carbonate is dissolving or precipitating, which PHREEQC should flag. For RQ4, thermal-water chloride has probably declined somewhat since the 1950 to 1991 baseline, consistent with decades of production, but the Cl/B signature of the thermal source should be essentially unchanged.

**Why several methods.** The four questions depend on each other. Major-ion and isotope chemistry identifies the thermal end-member and tests whether mixing is conservative (RQ1, RQ3). Fissure gas and PHREEQC modeling give an independent check on reservoir temperature and reaction state (RQ3, RQ4). Discharge and the chloride balance turn a concentration into a flux, which is what answers whether outflow has changed (RQ4). Time-series statistics turn a continuous conductance record and a sparse chloride record into a sampling design (RQ2). The calibration (RQ1) is what lets the other parts feed one continuously updated monitoring tool and not a one-time snapshot, and the same database and calculations can be reused the next time the system changes.

## Chloride and specific conductance as conservative-tracer proxies

Steamboat's thermal water is dominated by sodium and chloride, while background water in the area is dilute and richer in calcium and magnesium. Because chloride is conservative here, it traces the thermal fraction of a sample and, through a mass balance against stream discharge, the total thermal discharge [@sorey1992; @sorey2008; @sorey2017]. I propose specific conductance as a proxy because it is cheap, continuous and field-deployable, not because conductance itself is of interest. Whether the substitution holds across sites, seasons and the period before and after the 2025 eruption is the central empirical question, and the thesis tests it and does not assume it.

## Mass balances: chloride, heat and water

Three balances run through the thesis. The chloride balance asks how much thermal water enters a stream reach: chloride is conservative, so the difference between the chloride fluxes at two stations, divided by the thermal end-member concentration, is the thermal flow, provided the end-member and the discharges are known. The water balance asks the same of total flow, and in a creek that gains water from ditches and springs it separates thermal inflow from other inflow only through a tracer. The heat balance asks how much heat the reach gains, which for a stream with known inflow gives the temperature at which the thermal water entered. Each balance is only as good as its inputs, and each has a different weakness: the chloride balance depends on an end-member that has to be assumed, the water balance on stream gauges whose rating is uncertain by several percent, and the heat balance on thermometer readings and on heat lost to the air, which is neglected and so makes the inferred temperature a lower bound. They are most useful together. If a chloride-based inflow, a gauge-based inflow and a heat-based inflow temperature all point to the same system, the end-member and discharge assumptions are supported; if they disagree, the disagreement says which assumption to examine.

## The conductivity record so far

Two specific-conductance loggers have run in Steamboat Creek since 15 July 2026, one at the USGS gauge near Rhodes Road (SBRR, the upstream control) and one near Geiger Grade (SBGG, downstream). These are the same two roles Sorey and Spielman used for their chloride flux [@sorey2008; @sorey2017].

@fig-sbgg-install shows the SBGG logger after installation in July 2026, in a white PVC pipe, with a yellow line marking the cross-section used for repeat discharge measurements.

```{r fig-sbgg-install}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/field_photo_sbgg_install.jpg",
  "The SBGG (Geiger Grade) continuous specific-conductance logger, housed in the white PVC pipe at center, shortly after installation in Steamboat Creek (yellow line marks the discharge-measurement transect; capture date not preserved in this file).",
  alt = "Photograph of a white PVC logger housing standing in a shallow creek, with a yellow transect line and streamside willows.",
  id = "fig-sbgg-install"
)
```

Both loggers were re-downloaded on 12 October 2026, extending the record to 2026-10-10. When a logger is pulled from the stream and relaunched it reads air for a short time, which shows as a sharp, implausible drop in conductance (@fig-conductivity-timeseries). An automated screen flags those readings, and applied to the earlier download it reproduces every point I had flagged by hand.

The flagged points show only what the detector can see. Field observations indicate that each logger sat in air in its housing for at least several days before each pull as the stream dropped away from the sensor, and that interval cannot be separated from stream signal in the conductance record. Daily conductance stays smooth through the last days before the 10 October pull, and the daily temperature range widens only slightly, a weak hint since air temperature also drives it. The orange points therefore do not bound the valid data. Readings from the days before any retrieval are therefore provisional. The sampling-interval test below excludes the three days before each pull as a stated choice, and the calibration will use the same window until the length of exposure is established.

```{r fig-conductivity-timeseries}

  "output/figures/manuscript/conductivity_timeseries.png",
  "SBRR and SBGG conductivity record, 2026-07-15 to 2026-10-10. Orange points are readings the QC detector flagged at retrieval and relaunch events; the dashed line marks the last flagged reading. They do not bound the longer interval before each pull when the sensor sat partly or fully out of flowing water, which is not detectable in the conductance record.",
  alt = "Two-panel conductance time series at SBGG and SBRR, with orange points flagging readings at retrieval events.",
  id = "fig-conductivity-timeseries"
)
```
