## Evaluating conductance as a conservative proxy for chloride

Following Objective 2, every process capable of altering either
chloride or conductance independently is evaluated explicitly rather
than assumed away:

| Process | Alters chloride? | Alters conductance? |
|---|---|---|
| Dilution with meteoric water | Yes | Yes |
| Calcite/dolomite precipitation | No | Yes |
| Thermal/meteoric mixing | Yes | Yes |
| Silica precipitation | No | Slight |
| Ion exchange (sodium-calcium) | No | Slight to moderate |
| Evaporative concentration | Yes (concentrates) | Yes (concentrates), but in a different proportion than dilution/mixing |

Where a process alters conductance without a matching change in
chloride, that is a direct, falsifiable reason the proxy relationship
could fail at a given site or season, and this failure mode is
stated directly rather than smoothed over. The same framework is
then applied to any
outlier the eventual chloride-conductance calibration produces
(Objective 4): a sample sitting off the fitted relationship is checked
against this same process list before being treated as measurement
error.


## Chloride-conductivity calibration

This is the core analytical task, and it cannot be done yet because no chloride sample overlaps the logger record closely enough to form a calibration pair. Once paired samples exist (see the sampling plan below), I will regress chloride on specific conductance separately by site type (outlet, creek, monitoring well, spring) and compare each with a single global model, to see whether one relationship serves the whole system or each site needs its own. Reported uncertainty will include the regression's confidence interval and, where repeat sampling allows, an estimate of how much the relationship drifts across seasons.

**Model forms.** I will compare three forms, each for a stated reason. A linear regression of chloride on specific conductance (and temperature, if it improves the fit) is the simplest form and the one most comparable to how conductance has been used as a chloride proxy in other geothermal rivers [@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016]: $\text{Cl} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot SC + \beta_2 \cdot T + \varepsilon$, where $SC$ is specific conductance, $T$ is temperature and $\varepsilon$ is the unexplained error. A log-linear fit takes the log of chloride first, because chloride is positive and spans more than an order of magnitude from dilute background wells to the thermal end-member, and a plain linear fit can be pulled around by the highest values and predict negative chloride at the dilute end. A generalized additive model (GAM, fit with the mgcv package following @wood2017) replaces the single slope with a smooth curve $f(SC)$ estimated from the data, so the relation can bend where the data require it without chasing noise. A random forest (ranger package, following @breiman2001) serves as a benchmark and not as the reported calibration, since it returns no equation a field technician could apply by hand. It sets an upper bound on the skill a very flexible model can extract from the same predictors. If it clearly beats the three simpler forms, the relation has structure they miss, such as a threshold that depends on site type, and the calibration would need to be revisited. The comparison is already built and has been run only on simulated data standing in for the paired samples.

**Validation.** Chloride and conductance are both autocorrelated, so ordinary random cross-validation would leak information between nearly identical neighboring observations and overstate skill. Each model is instead scored with rolling-origin (time-ordered) cross-validation, following @bergmeir2012: each fold trains only on data up to a point in time and tests on the data just after it, which mirrors how the calibration will be used. The score is the cross-validated root mean square error (RMSE, the typical size of a prediction error in chloride units) and mean absolute error averaged across folds, not an in-sample fit.

**Global or site-specific model.** The candidate forms come from different model families, so the main comparison is cross-validated RMSE under the same scheme, the one criterion valid across all of them. Where two models are nested, for example a linear or GAM model with and without a site-type term, AIC and a likelihood-ratio test are reported as a secondary check. A site-specific model is adopted over the global one only if it improves cross-validated RMSE by more than the fold-to-fold variability.

## Minimum sampling-frequency design via Monte Carlo subsampling

This analysis serves RQ2 and is already done. No dense chloride record exists, so it uses the densely sampled conductance record as a stand-in and asks how much is lost by sampling it sparsely, in conductance units. The quantity of interest in the end is mass flux, $F = \int C(t)\,Q(t)\,dt$, where $C$ is chloride concentration and $Q$ is discharge. The same procedure computes a flux error when a paired discharge series is supplied, using trapezoidal integration, and will report it once discharge is paired with the logger record.

**The method.** For each candidate interval (1, 2, 3, 7 and 14 days) I (1) draw a random start day within the first interval; (2) subsample the dense conductance record at that interval, as if a campaign had sampled every N days starting on that day; (3) linearly interpolate between those sparse points to rebuild the record; (4) compare the rebuilt record with the full one, as a root mean square error in percent of the mean; and (5) repeat 200 times with new random start days. The repetition is what makes it a Monte Carlo test. A schedule that happens to catch every daily peak or every trough looks better or worse than one that samples evenly, and 200 random starts show that spread directly (@fig-mcspread) instead of reporting one number that might reflect a lucky start.

**Result, with air-exposed readings removed.** I removed (1) readings the QC screen flagged as retrieval artifacts or spikes, (2) the three days before each retrieval, because field notes show the loggers sat in air for at least several days before each pull, and (3) the SBGG record from 29 September 2026, when the logger began to be exposed to air (its daily temperature range rises from about 5 C to 7 to 8 C that day). These readings are instrument artifacts, and leaving them in would inflate the error for reasons unrelated to sampling frequency. The three-day window is a stated choice, because the exposure cannot be seen in the conductance itself. Widening it to seven days or moving the SBGG onset to 25 September or 2 October changes the mean error by no more than about 0.6 percentage points. Daily sampling gives a mean error of 3.6% of mean conductance at SBRR and 3.1% at SBGG, every other day 4.3% and 4.1%, weekly 6.9% and 7.8%, and biweekly 9.5% and 8.5%. The error grows smoothly with no cliff, so the interval is a trade between precision and cost. The worst case (95th percentile of the 200 campaigns) grows faster: at SBRR it is 4.0% daily, 4.8% every other day, 7.7% weekly and 12.1% biweekly, and at SBGG 5.0%, 5.0%, 9.8% and 13.2%. Going from daily to every other day therefore costs little in the typical case, while a weekly or biweekly schedule can land well above the mean depending on the start day (@fig-mc and @fig-mcspread). A biweekly campaign could land anywhere from about 7% to 13% depending only on its start day, which is the reason for a short daily window ahead of any coarser interval. This is the basis for the sampling design below.

**What has and has not been run on measured data.** The Monte Carlo result is the only analysis run on the measured record, and it alone sets the sampling interval. The linear, GAM and random-forest chloride models have not been fit to measured pairs, because no chloride sample overlaps the logger record. They have only been run as a code test on simulated data: 60 samples every three days from 1 May 2026, with $SC = 300 + 40\sin(2\pi d/365) + \mathrm{N}(0,15)$, $T = 15 + 8\sin(2\pi (d-60)/365) + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5)$ and $\mathrm{Cl} = 1 + 0.071\,SC_{lag} + 0.1\,T_{lag} + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5)$, with a six-day lag. The slope 0.071 comes from the single measured SBRR pair (Cl 17.1 mg/L at 241 uS/cm on 2026-05-01), and every other number is made up. Because the data come from a known linear rule, the exercise shows only that the fitting and cross-validation code runs and recovers a known relation. It says nothing about how a GAM will perform on Steamboat Creek and did not influence the interval. The only available fit, a linear regression on 181 historical NDEP pairs at Rhodes Road (1987 to 2025, $R^2 = 0.65$), predates the loggers.

**Proposed sampling design.** I propose a chloride campaign at the two logger stations, SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) and SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream), because they are the only places where a chloride sample can be paired with a running conductance record. Since no sample overlaps the deployment yet, the first task is a short, daily to sub-daily window of two to four weeks at both stations. The loggers have run since mid-July 2026, so there is no reason to wait for a spring field season, and I plan to start this fall or winter. After the window, I would sample roughly monthly at both stations from December through September, about ten months ending in early fall, which covers winter low flow, spring runoff, summer baseflow and the fall transition, with extra samples around large storms and spring snowmelt, when the relation is most likely to break down. Starting earlier turns the seasonal-stability question in RQ1 from a hypothesis into something I can test, instead of extrapolating from the twelve-week summer and early fall record that the Monte Carlo test has to use. Every calibration sample should carry major ions, and a subset should carry delta-18-O and delta-D isotopes, since chloride alone cannot tell mixing from evaporative concentration. A practical minimum of 15 to 20 pairs supports a stable regression, and the window plus ten months of monthly sampling clears the more defensible target of 30 to 40 pairs without relying on one season. @tbl-samplingplan gives the design by site, analyte set and frequency.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\footnotesize
```

| Site | What is sampled | Frequency / timing | Why |
|------------------|----------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) | Chloride, major ions (Na, K, Ca, Mg, SO4, alkalinity), field pH/temperature/specific conductance | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks (intensive window, starting fall/winter 2026) | Establishes the calibration's short-timescale behavior and its noise floor against the logger's own continuous record. |
| SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream) | Same analyte set as SBRR | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks, concurrent with the SBRR window | A second, independently calibrated site tests whether one relationship serves the whole system (RQ1) or whether SBRR and SBGG need their own equations. |
| SBRR and SBGG | Same analyte set as above | Monthly, from December through September (about ten months, ending in early fall) following the intensive window | Tests seasonal stability (RQ1) across winter baseflow, spring runoff, summer baseflow, and fall transition, not just one season. |
| SBRR and SBGG (opportunistic) | Same analyte set as above | Additional unscheduled samples around large storms and spring snowmelt | These are the conditions most likely to break the conservative-mixing assumption (dilution, flashy runoff); oversampled rather than left to chance. |
| A prioritized subset of the above (SBRR and SBGG) | delta-18-O / delta-D isotopes | Roughly one isotope sample per season, timed with a regular chloride visit | Chloride alone cannot distinguish simple thermal/meteoric mixing from evaporative concentration (both raise chloride); isotopes can. |

: Proposed chloride sampling plan at the two conductivity-logger
stations. {#tbl-samplingplan}

## Post-eruption chloride-flux monitoring

Following RQ4, the chloride mass-balance method is applied to every
date on which chloride and discharge are both available at the two gauging
stations, and the result is compared against the full historical record
(White's 1950s/1960s estimates, Sorey and Spielman's 2008-2016 values, and
the 2026 poster estimate) to ask whether outflow has measurably changed
since the eruption, while explicitly accounting for the seasonal
variability Sorey and Spielman themselves documented at these same sites.
The same conservative-ratio tracking used for endmember stability (above)
is applied here as a second, independent line of evidence: a stable ratio
across the eruption itself would support continuity of the same source
fluid, while a shift would support a change in fluid provenance or mixing
pathway.

**A database-grounded discharge estimate.** Applying the
chloride mass-balance method to the one date with paired
chloride and discharge measurements at both gauging stations gives
58.7 liters per second, a single-day value that sits within, not
clearly above or below, the broader 1955-2026 record (roughly
30-90 L/s depending on year and method) once Sorey and Spielman's own
documented seasonal variability is taken into account, shown in
@fig-discharge.

**A three-month field-parameter time series.** A roughly monthly
record of pH, temperature, and specific conductance across fourteen sites
(six injection-side ports and eight shallow monitoring and domestic wells)
spanning late September through December 2025 shows a stable, consistent
gap between the injection-side ports (pH 5.8-6.3) and the shallow well
network (pH 7.0-8.1), present in every round rather than as a single-date
artifact. Two individual wells also show opposite-direction
multi-month trends not explained by any change in the other monitored
parameter at the same well, a pattern that cautions against treating any
single field parameter as a universal proxy for thermal fraction across the
whole system.

## Uncertainty in the chloride-based discharge

The thermal inflow between SBRR and SBBV is computed as

$$
Q_{TW} = \frac{Q_{BV}\,C_{BV} - Q_{RR}\,C_{RR}}{C_{TW}},
$$

where $Q$ is stream discharge, $C$ is chloride concentration, the subscripts mark the downstream station (BV), the upstream station (RR) and the thermal end-member (TW), and the end-member concentration is 820 mg/L following Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992]. The uncertainty of $Q_{TW}$ follows from adding the relative errors of each term in quadrature. As planning values, and not measured errors, take 10 percent for each stream discharge, 5 percent for each laboratory chloride value and 3 percent for the end-member concentration. The two chloride fluxes on 1 May 2026 are then 53.5 g/s (SBBV) and 5.4 g/s (SBRR), each uncertain by about 11 percent; their difference, 48.1 g/s, is uncertain by about 6.0 g/s (12.5 percent), and with the end-member term the thermal inflow is 58.7 plus or minus about 7.6 L/s (13 percent). The upstream term is small, so the result is controlled by the downstream discharge and chloride. The 1 May samples were taken shortly before Steamboat Ditch began to carry water, so the ditch was not adding water below SBRR on that date and does not bias this estimate. Three consequences follow. A change in thermal inflow smaller than about 15 percent cannot be separated from measurement error on a single date. The 1 May value and the poster's 27 L/s average differ by more than this error, but they are not the same quantity (one date against an average over several), so the comparison does not yet say that discharge changed. And the largest single improvement available is better discharge at SBBV, which is why the proposal asks for a flow measurement or a rated station at the downstream logger.

## The sampling plan in depth: calibration pairs, the Monte Carlo design, and Lower Terrace mapping

Sampling serves three purposes in this thesis, and the plan is built so that one visit serves all three: pairing chloride with conductance for the calibration (RQ1), setting how often chloride must be measured (RQ2), and characterizing the discharge points of the Lower Sinter Terrace so that the thermal map can be tied to chemistry (RQ3 and RQ4).

**What the Monte Carlo test establishes, and what it does not.** @tbl-mcsummary repeats the result from the previous section with air-exposed days removed. The test covers the concentration signal only and not mass flux, because no discharge record overlaps the loggers yet, and it measures how well a sparse sample reproduces conductance, not chloride. It is therefore the basis for the interval and not a test of the calibration itself.

| Sampling interval | SBRR mean (%) | SBRR 95th percentile (%) | SBGG mean (%) | SBGG 95th percentile (%) |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Daily | 3.6 | 4.0 | 3.1 | 5.0 |
| Every other day | 4.3 | 4.8 | 4.1 | 5.0 |
| Weekly | 6.9 | 7.7 | 7.8 | 9.8 |
| Biweekly | 9.5 | 12.1 | 8.5 | 13.2 |

: Reconstruction error of the conductance record as a percent of its mean, over 200 random campaigns per interval, with air-exposure days removed. {#tbl-mcsummary}

**Calibration pairs.** The design is an intensive daily to sub-daily window followed by monthly sampling from December through September (about ten months, ending in early fall) (@tbl-samplingplan). A reasoned minimum is 15-20 pairs for a stable regression and 30-40 for a seasonally defensible one, and a tier of about 40 analyses is recommended for a one-person thesis. This is a reasoned count, not a power analysis, because no chloride-conductance pairs exist yet to compute one against. Pairing chloride with the major ions lets the mixing model be checked in the same samples, and about one isotope sample per season at the two creek stations is the only way to separate evaporation from conservative mixing.

**The Steamboat Ditch season and the upstream station.** Steamboat Ditch joins Steamboat Creek just below SBRR and, from about May to September, supplies much of the flow in the creek below that point. This comes from field knowledge and still has to be confirmed by measuring the ditch and the creek at the first visits; it is not documented in the earlier chloride work at this site. If it holds, SBRR in summer is a low-flow, possibly stagnant reach above the confluence, and its water is not the water that enters the thermal reach. It then cannot serve as the background (pre-discharge) station for the chloride balance in that season. The provisional flux for July to October used SBRR as the upstream term and is limited in this way, so it is treated as a bound. The 1 May 2026 estimate is not affected: SBRR was flowing when it was sampled, shortly before the ditch began to carry water, so the ditch was not adding water below the station on that date.

The proposed refinement has three parts. First, when the ditch is carrying water (about May to September), the upstream station would be a site just below the confluence, where one station records the combined creek and ditch water; because that water is already summed there, no separate ditch term is needed in the balance, which stays $Q_{TW} = (Q_d C_d - Q_u C_u) / C_{TW}$. When the ditch is off, SBRR remains the upstream station, as before. Second, the downstream logger (SBGG) would move upstream, closer to the terrace, to a point above the Cranes Ditch diversion. The reason is low flow at SBGG: dirt infill in Steamboat Creek before September 2026 lowered the flow at that site and affected the downstream logger, which began to be exposed to open air in late September (its daily temperature range rose from about 5 C to 7 to 8 C from 2026-09-29), so the later readings are excluded from the sampling-interval test. A site above the Cranes Ditch diversion should keep enough flow over the logger. Third, one field day with a hydrologist would measure channel transects (width, depth and velocity) at both new locations, so that discharge can be measured by the velocity-area method and a stage-discharge relation built where there is no gauge.

In summer the new upstream site will not be co-located with USGS gauge 10349300, as SBRR was, so discharge there will come from manual measurements at each calibration visit and from the relation built from them. Ditch discharge and chloride would also be measured just above the confluence at a few early visits, to confirm that the ditch water is low in chloride. The summer record from the new site cannot be treated as continuous with the 2026 SBRR record, so the old and new locations should overlap for a short period if possible. The dates when the ditch carries water and the location of the Cranes Ditch diversion are to be confirmed in the field.

**Mapping the Lower Terrace.** @tbl-lstsampling lists proposed sampling by source, with the sources taken from the thermal map. The counts are a starting point to be fitted to the laboratory budget and to site access, and they come in addition to the roughly 40 calibration analyses.

```{=latex}

```

| Source (from the thermal map) | Why | Proposed samples per year | Measurements |
|-------------------|-----------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| Fissure zone (SBF_0001, SBF_0002, NV26-1) | Deep-source end-member; gas repeat | 4 water (quarterly), 2 gas | Major ions, boron, lithium, silica, 2 isotope samples; gas composition |
| Lower Terrace channel (largest anomaly, 161 m^2^) | Whether it shares the fissure's source | 4 (quarterly), access permitting | Major ions, silica, field temperature, pH, conductance |
| Creek-corridor springs and seeps (17 polygons; SBS_0001, SBS_0002, SBS_0006; springs 45, 46, 44e and 50n by alias) | Diffuse thermal inflow to the creek | 12 (6 springs, 2 seasons) | Chloride, major ions, field parameters |
| Resort tank and overflow, with the creek above and below the entry point | Resort share of the thermal inflow | 12 (4 dates, 3 points) | Chloride, conductance, temperature, flow |
| Capped eruption pipe (SBW_0003), if accessible | The 2025 eruption pipe | 2 | Major ions, temperature, water level |

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

**Repeat thermal surveys.** The 488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius is a baseline. If NBMG can repeat the calibrated drone flights each season, the same pixel to polygon method gives a change metric (area by source and season) at no laboratory cost, and a repeat of the October 2025 flight would show whether the creek-corridor springs and the fissure zone are growing, shrinking or moving.

**Decision rules.** After the first full cycle, residuals are compared by season and site type. A single calibration is kept only if its error is acceptable against a threshold set explicitly with the committee (no default threshold is assumed); otherwise site-specific equations are reported with their uncertainty, as RQ1's deliverable states.

## From the 2026 record to a proposed change in locations

The 2026 record led to the refinement described under the Steamboat Ditch season above: use SBRR as the upstream station only when the ditch is off, use a station below the confluence with manual discharge measurements in summer, and move SBGG upstream above the Cranes Ditch diversion. Until that is done and chloride samples overlap the loggers, the July to October flux remains a bound; the 1 May 2026 estimate was taken before the ditch carried water and stands as measured.

# Schedule, costs, and program of study {#sec-costs}



The schedule below moves the intensive calibration window up to this
fall/winter (rather than a conventional spring field-season start) and
stretches monthly chloride sampling from December through September (about ten months, ending in early fall), so the
calibration can be tested against all four seasons before it is
treated as final, consistent with the sampling-design reasoning above.
Target dates are a planning structure, not fixed commitments, and will
be adjusted against the academic calendar and committee
availability as the work proceeds. The most direct risk to this
schedule is weather- or access-limited fieldwork during the
fall/winter calibration window; the contingency is the same ten-month
monthly cadence shifted later into spring/summer 2027, at the cost of
testing fewer distinct seasons before the calibration is finalized.
A second risk is that the chloride-conductance relationship
turns out to be too noisy or site-specific to support a single
practical calibration; the contingency there is reported directly in
RQ1's own deliverable above (site-specific equations with stated
uncertainty, not a forced single model) rather than treated as a
schedule failure.

@fig-schedule sets the plan against what is already on file. The long records (weather and pressure from 1938, chemistry from 1950, water levels from 1952) are the historical frame; the continuous logger records are short, which is the reason the calibration window starts now and not in a later field season. ## Proposed costs and timeline

Costs fall into three groups: laboratory analyses, which are the largest budgeted item; field logistics and equipment; and support that is expected in kind from NBMG, UNR and collaborators. Laboratory prices come from the invoice for the samples I have already had analyzed: one batch of seven, run for the super-trace water package (ME-MS14L) and anions by ion chromatography (MS14L-ANPH). Login, disposal and the two analyses are charged per sample. The administration fee is treated as charged once per batch, but I am not sure of that, and shipping to the laboratory is not on the invoice, so the estimates carry a range: the central value assumes the fee is per batch, $35 per shipment, and biweekly samples held and shipped monthly; the low and high values change the fee to per sample, shipping to $20 or $50, and shipments to one per visit. Isotopes are run outside that laboratory and the $40 per sample is a planning estimate. Ten percent of samples are added for duplicates and blanks.

The Lower Terrace work in @tbl-lstsampling adds 34 analyses plus 4 duplicates and blanks, four shipments, and 2 isotope samples, about `r fmt_usd(lt_cost)` (range `r fmt_usd(lt_range[1])` to `r fmt_usd(lt_range[2])`). With that added, the central laboratory total is about `r fmt_usd(so$total[2] + lt_cost)` for monthly sampling with isotopes, `r fmt_usd(so$total[4] + lt_cost)` for biweekly sampling with isotopes, and `r fmt_usd(so$total[5] + lt_cost)` for the fissure-centered option. Biweekly with isotopes is my working choice, and monthly without isotopes (`r fmt_usd(so$total[1] + lt_cost)`) is the fallback if funding is short. The fissure-centered option is the most informative for the question of how changes at the source reach the creek and costs about `r fmt_usd(so$total[5] - so$total[4])` more than B2; it can be trimmed by sampling fewer fissure-area sites.

**Calibration window and later sampling priced separately.** The intensive window (daily, 2 to 4 weeks) and the monthly or biweekly sampling that follows are separate parts of the plan. With the central prices, a 14-day window costs about `r fmt_usd(phase_split()$phase1_cost[5])` in the laboratory and the monthly (A1) and biweekly with isotopes (B2) phases cost about `r fmt_usd(phase_split()$phase2_cost[5])` and `r fmt_usd(phase_split()$phase2_cost[8])`, so the two together are about `r fmt_usd(phase_split()$combined[5])` to `r fmt_usd(phase_split()$combined[8])`. A 7-day window lowers the combined figure by about $2,600. SBGG also needs a manual discharge measurement at each visit, which is field time and not a laboratory charge.

**What the baseline says about detecting change.** The mixing results give each Lower Terrace feature a fingerprint: its chloride, its fraction of fissure water (from chloride, with SBRR as the dilute end), and its Cl/B and Na/Cl ratios. If two single samples are compared and each carries a 5 percent analytical error, a difference below about 14 percent in chloride cannot be told from chance, which is a change of 0.08 to 0.15 in the fissure fraction depending on the feature (the well SBW_0001 is the most sensitive, the fissure and resort tank the least). The ratios are less useful than hoped. Cl/B runs only from 20 to 23 across the features and Na/Cl from 0.77 to 0.85, differences smaller than the roughly 20 percent that two single ratios could differ by chance, so the ratios cannot yet separate the features from one another. They can still show a large change in the source, and they are the check that tells dilution (chloride moves, ratios do not) from a change in the fluid (ratios move) once repeat samples tighten the baseline.

**What a change at the springs or fissure would look like at the creek.** At SBBV, thermal water is about 14 percent of the flow but about 86 percent of the chloride, so a fractional change in the thermal chloride flux shows up in creek chloride almost one for one. With the analytical error and a 9 percent reconstruction error for the biweekly record, a single creek comparison would need a change of about 33 percent in thermal chloride flux to stand out. Averaging the ten or so samples taken in each period lowers that to roughly 10 percent, which is why the repeat sampling matters more than any single round. These are planning numbers from one snapshot and no replicates, not tests, and replicate samples at the first visits will replace the assumed 5 percent.

**Why a fissure-centered tier.** Option C adds four sites near the fissure (the capped pipe and fissure vent, SBW_0001, SBS_0001 and SBW_0002) to the biweekly creek program, sampled monthly with isotopes. The reason is that the creek only integrates the thermal inflow, and the sites above it are where a change in the source would appear first and in a form (ratios, silica, isotopes) that the creek chloride cannot show. A change at the fissure that is followed by a change in creek chloride and in the SBRR to SBBV chloride flux would link the two; a change at the creek with no change at the fissure and springs would point to dilution or to inflow from somewhere else. The figure shows the baseline each of these would be compared against.

# Geochemical modeling with PHREEQC {#sec-phreeqc}

The proxy depends on chloride and conductance moving together, and that assumption needs a chemical check. This chapter uses PHREEQC, a geochemical modeling program, as a supporting tool and not as a thesis in itself. It reconstructs the deep fluid from the fissure gas and water samples, follows how that fluid changes as it reaches the springs and wells of the Lower Terrace, and mixes it with creek water to see how the chemistry at the terrace turns into the chemistry measured at the creek stations SBRR and SBBV. The same mixing framework gives a thermal outflow, which is compared with the earlier estimates of Sorey and Spielman and of Collar. For readers outside geochemistry, each calculation is described by what it asks and what it can and cannot show.


## Major-ion chemistry: what each analyte tells us

| Analyte | Role in this system |
|---|---|
| Chloride | The primary conservative tracer. |
| Sodium, potassium | Track with chloride in the thermal end-member; also the basis of sodium/potassium geothermometry (below). |
| Sulfate | Also strongly correlated with chloride, sodium, and potassium here (a secondary conservative-ish tracer, though sulfate can be affected by anhydrite/gypsum equilibria at high enough concentration). |
| Calcium, magnesium | Behave oppositely to the chloride/sodium/potassium group; track a more dilute, rock-reacted water-rock interaction signature. |
| Alkalinity | Drives carbonate mineral saturation (calcite, dolomite, aragonite). |
| Boron, lithium, fluoride | Minor conservative-ish tracers used for independent cross-checks, such as the chloride to boron ratio discussed below. |
| Silica | The basis of quartz/chalcedony geothermometry; behaves less conservatively than sodium/potassium on the ascent-to-discharge path at Steamboat. |

## Charge balance and mineral saturation

Every water analysis is first screened for internal consistency via
the standard charge-balance-error statistic,

$$
\text{CBE\%} = \frac{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} - \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}}
{\sum z_i m_i^{\text{cation}} + \sum |z_i| m_i^{\text{anion}}} \times 100,
$$

where $z_i$ and $m_i$ are the charge and molar concentration of each
ion; a sample passing within $\pm 5\%$ is analytically reliable
enough to model further. The mineral saturation index then
quantifies how far a water is from equilibrium with a given mineral,

$$
SI = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{IAP}{K_{sp}}\right),
$$

where $IAP$ is the ion activity product computed from the sample's
speciated chemistry and $K_{sp}$ is that mineral's temperature-
dependent solubility product; $SI = 0$ is equilibrium, $SI > 0$
implies a tendency to precipitate (scale), and $SI < 0$ implies a
tendency to dissolve.

## Geothermometry: two independent, and divergent, temperature estimates

Activity-based sodium/potassium geothermometers estimate the deep
reservoir temperature a water last equilibrated with, from the ratio
of sodium to potassium activity. Two widely used forms are
Giggenbach's [@giggenbach1988]

$$
T_{\text{Gigg}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1390}{1.75 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15
$$

and Fournier's [@fournier1979]

$$
T_{\text{Four}}(^\circ C) = \frac{1217}{1.483 + \log_{10}(a_{Na}/a_K)} - 273.15 .
$$

Silica (quartz/chalcedony) geothermometry instead uses dissolved
silica's own temperature-dependent solubility, read from the
equilibrium temperature at which a mineral's saturation index crosses
zero. At Steamboat, sodium/potassium estimates (154-256 degrees
Celsius) systematically and substantially exceed quartz/chalcedony
estimates (52-127 degrees Celsius). This divergence is real and
informative, not a contradiction: silica re-
equilibrates toward ambient conditions faster than the sodium/
potassium ratio does as water cools and dilutes on its way to
discharge, so the two geothermometers are expected to diverge exactly
this way along a single cooling, diluting flow path. This
divergence as evidence approach follows Shevenell and De Rocher's
[@shevenell2005] own evaluation of multiple geothermometers across
several Nevada geothermal power plants, which found that no single
geothermometer is reliable in isolation and that comparing several
against each other is itself diagnostic of a system's mixing and
cooling history, not just a single reservoir-temperature estimate.

## How PHREEQC is used here

PHREEQC [@phreeqc] is an open-source program that solves aqueous speciation, mineral saturation, mixing and mass-balance problems from a water analysis and a thermodynamic database. I do not treat it as a modeling exercise of its own. It answers four questions that serve the chloride-conductance proxy. The first is water types: major-ion chemistry, principal components and hydrochemical clustering separate a thermal end-member (outlet and thermal-well samples), mixed waters (monitoring wells with partial dilution) and dilute background waters (domestic wells). The second is conservative behavior: whether carbonate or silica precipitation, ion exchange or evaporation could change conductance independently of chloride, as laid out in the process table in the proxy chapter. The third is end-member stability: whether the equilibrium behavior, and not just the composition, of the thermal end-member in the 1950s, the 1990s and now has stayed the same, which bears on whether a calibration fit today holds backward or forward in time. The fourth is outliers: why a sample that falls off the calibration deviates, whether from dilution, mineral precipitation, mixing with another water or an unusual pH, which is more informative than a table of saturation indices.

## What PHREEQC can and cannot tell us

PHREEQC answers one kind of question: if this water sits in contact with these minerals and this gas, what does its chemistry settle into? It does not know where in the ground the water is, how fast it moves, or how far it travels. Every calculation here (speciation, saturation index, mixing, forward reaction-path titration) treats a sample as a single well-mixed parcel, which is called a batch or zero-dimensional model. A reactive-transport model adds a spatial grid and a flow field so that chemistry can be followed as water moves through rock. Such tools exist, including PHAST (PHREEQC's chemistry coupled to a 3-D flow model, from the USGS), TOUGHREACT and CrunchFlow. I use none of them, because they need a calibrated permeability field, effective porosity, reservoir boundary conditions and a transient pressure history, and none of these exists for Steamboat at the needed resolution. A model built now would be dominated by untested assumptions.

This limits how the results should be read. A forward titration that finds a net dissolution of about one-tenth of a millimole of calcite and dolomite says how much carbonate chemistry had to be added or removed to match a sample, not where, over what distance or how fast. A two end-member mixing fraction says what proportion of two waters would explain a sample's chloride, not the path the water took. Even so, a batch model can make useful distinctions. It shows that SBS_0001 cannot be explained by the mixing and carbonate reaction that explains its four downgradient neighbors, although SBS_0001 and one of them are only 109 m apart. A fault, a different flow path or a different rock unit would each fit that result, and only spatial and structural data could tell them apart. A 3-D geologic model therefore has a place here only as conceptual context for where the wells sit relative to structure and lithology, and not as a platform for simulating flow.

## PHREEQC workflow: sample eligibility, databases, and interpretation

A sample is run through PHREEQC only if it has pH, temperature and the major ions (chloride, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and alkalinity), with a field value preferred over a laboratory one. Of the samples in the database, 404 meet that test. Laboratory alkalinity is reported as calcium carbonate and is converted to bicarbonate before use. Each sample is run against a thermodynamic database chosen for its temperature and salinity, with the others as a fallback if the model will not converge. The charge balance is checked first, and the saturation indices, speciation and geothermometer temperatures are then read from the output. The full workflow, the mixing, inverse-model and gas-phase options, and the checks that caught errors are in Appendix A.

## Fissure gas geochemistry

In April 2026 T. Fischer and K. Mtili (UCSB), with P. Ruprecht, collected three free-gas samples at the Lower Sinter Terrace fissure and an adjacent degassing area across the road. Dry-gas composition and carbon isotopes were analyzed at Fischer's Volatiles Lab (UCSB) and noble-gas ratios at P. Barry's lab (WHOI). This is the first gas dataset I have, and the only Steamboat gas chemistry on file besides Mariner and Janik's [-@mariner1995] 1991 to 1994 analyses of well 23-5. One sample (NV26-2) has a flagged contamination risk: the field team noted a possible Giggenbach-bottle leak, and it was collected where gas was escaping through fresh asphalt. It is treated separately below.

Near-surface vent gas is never air-free, so each sample is first corrected for atmospheric entrainment, assuming the measured O2 is all atmospheric: air-derived N2 is estimated from the dry-air N2/O2 ratio (3.773) and subtracted, and the rest is renormalized. The D'Amore and Panichi [-@damore1980] multicomponent gas geothermometer is then run on each corrected composition.

The air-corrected ratios (CO2/N2, H2S/CO2, N2/Ar, CH4/CO2) for NV26-1 and NV26-3 fall within or near the range Mariner and Janik report for well 23-5 three decades earlier (@fig-gascomp), while NV26-2 sits well outside it, consistent with its flagged contamination. The gas-geothermometer estimates for NV26-1 and NV26-3 (228 and 181 C) bracket Mariner and Janik's well 23-5 range (173 to 200 C) (@fig-gastherm), and for all three samples they sit well above the measured vent temperatures (96 to 99.5 C). That is the same cooling, diluting flow-path pattern seen in the water geothermometers. NV26-1 is co-located with SBF_0001, a water sample collected on 1 May 2026 with complete major-ion and isotope chemistry (chloride 815 mg/L, delta-18-O -12.3 per mil, delta-D -114 per mil), the first point with both gas and water chemistry from one location. NV26-2's problem is a lesson for the sampling plan: future gas sampling at the terrace should avoid breaking through fresh pavement and should check bottle seals before leaving the site.

## A gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction and flowpath trace

NV26-1's gas is paired with sample 816 (SBF_0001, the fissure water), the only water-gas pair I have. A first-pass, simplified reconstruction works backward from each measured (post-boiling) fluid to a likely pre-boiling parent composition, then traces both forward to the creek. The reservoir temperature comes from the Giggenbach Na/K geothermometer, not quartz or chalcedony, which sit below the measured discharge temperature here. A single-step adiabatic enthalpy balance, using steam-table enthalpies, gives the fraction of the parent's mass lost as steam between reservoir and discharge temperature. The conservative species (chloride, sodium, potassium, sulfate, boron, lithium, bromide, fluoride, strontium and alkalinity) are scaled back by one minus the steam-loss fraction, since boiling concentrates the residual liquid. NV26-1's air-corrected CO2 to H2S ratio then seeds a PHREEQC gas-phase equilibration at the reservoir saturation pressure (several atmospheres), which resets pH and carbonate speciation to a plausible pre-boiling state. The method assumes single-step boiling and that CO2 and H2S go entirely into the escaping vapor, and it applies the one gas sample to both the fissure and the resort-tank water because no gas sample exists at the tank. It is a first pass meant to be refined.

For the fissure (sample 816) it gives a steam-loss fraction of 19.4 percent (reservoir 173.4 C, measured discharge 67.0 C), a parent chloride of 657 mg/L (below the measured 815 because boiling concentrates the liquid), and, after re-equilibration with NV26-1's gas at the reservoir pressure of 8.7 atmospheres, a more acidic parent pH of 5.5 (measured 8.3) with calcite and dolomite saturation indices that flip from mildly supersaturated to clearly undersaturated (@fig-parentfluid). That is the expected direction for a deep, gas-charged fluid that has not yet degassed: carbonate scaling is a shallow effect that appears as CO2 escapes and pH rises. The resort-tank sample (815) gives a similar steam loss (20.8 percent) and a parent chloride within 2.3 percent of the fissure's (657 and 672 mg/L). I report that agreement and do not rely on it. The resort tank is pumped by an intermittent air-lift, a forced-aeration process that the steam-loss physics does not represent, so its reconstructed parent is not a trustworthy estimate of a deep fluid, and the agreement could be coincidence. Potassium, sulfate, lithium and strontium agree less well (9 to 15 percent apart). The resort tank's gas-equilibration step did not converge at its measured pH of 9.0, so I report only its conservative-species concentrations.

```{r fig-parentfluid}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/parent_fluid_comparison.png",
  "A. Measured versus gas-informed reconstructed parent-fluid composition for the fissure sample. B. The resulting conservative-chloride thermal mixing fraction for three Lower Sinter Terrace samples, computed with the measured fluid versus the reconstructed parent fluid as the thermal end-member.",
  alt = "Two panels: measured versus parent-fluid concentrations of ten conservative species, and mixing fractions under two end-member choices.",
  id = "fig-parentfluid"
)
```

**What the further modeling shows.** Inverse models find a feasible two end-member plus carbonate solution for SBW_0001 only when the allowed analytical uncertainty is loosened to 12 percent, and a forward titration of calcite and dolomite agrees on the sign and size of the correction, a net dissolution of a few times 1e-4 mol (@fig-reactionpath). Against the three Lower Terrace springs the same titration fits SBS_0002 and SBS_0003 well and SBS_0001 poorly (@fig-reactionpath-comparison), a distinction a proximity map cannot give. The Na/K, quartz and gas geothermometers agree on a shared deep reservoir near 175 to 190 C, with the quartz estimates showing more near-surface cooling at the springs than at the wells (@fig-geothermwatergas), and equilibrating the fissure water with its own gas lowers the pH from 8.3 to 5.7 (@fig-gasphase), so the water as sampled is not in equilibrium with the vent gas. The details, with the supporting figures, are in Appendix A.

**From parent fluid to the creek.** @fig-evolution puts the two reconstructed parent fluids, the measured fissure and resort-tank chemistry, a nearby well (SBW_0001) and the two creek chloride-balance stations (SBRR, then downstream SBBV) on one flowpath. Chloride, sodium, silica and boron fall in the same order along it: high at the parent, fissure and resort tank, about half at SBW_0001, near background at SBRR, and measurably higher again at SBBV. The SBRR to SBBV difference is the same chloride-flux difference that drives the thermal-discharge estimate, now shown constituent by constituent. pH rises from the acidic reconstructed parent through the alkaline, partly degassed discharge points to the near-neutral creek, as expected with progressive CO2 loss. Calcite is undersaturated at the parent, mildly supersaturated at the two discharge points and most supersaturated at the nearby well and creek, which shows where scaling risk is highest. The quartz geothermometer falls smoothly along the same sequence (118 and 99 C at the two warmest points down to 53 to 62 C at the creek). The Na/K geothermometer does not behave this way at the creek stations (implausible 195 to 255 C), a known artifact of applying it to dilute, non-thermal water, and is shown only for transparency. Oxygen and hydrogen isotopes place both creek stations close together and more depleted than the fissure or resort tank, consistent with thermal inflow that is small enough to shift chloride measurably while barely moving a bulk isotope signature dominated by meteoric water.

```{r fig-evolution}
  "output/figures/manuscript/fluid_evolution_flowpath.png",
  "Chemistry, PHREEQC saturation indices, geothermometer estimates, and stable isotopes across the sampled Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath, from the two reconstructed parent fluids through measured discharge, a nearby well, and the two Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations.",
  alt = "Twelve-panel scatter of major ions, boron, pH, saturation indices, geothermometers and isotopes across the flowpath nodes.",
  id = "fig-evolution"
)
```

@fig-conceptual summarizes the flowpath as a schematic, from the deep parent fluid through degassing, the three measured discharge points and shallow mixing to the creek at SBRR, White's [-@white1968c] documented inflow of about 100 gallons per minute of "unseen" thermal water between SBRR and SBBV, and the downstream logger and gauge. The thermal imagery suggests at least two physically distinct discharge styles side by side on the terrace, which is a testable prediction for the remapping.

```{r fig-conceptual}

  "output/figures/manuscript/lst_conceptual_flowpath.png",
  "Conceptual flowpath from the reconstructed deep parent fluid through degassing, the three measured discharge points, shallow meteoric mixing, Steamboat Creek, and the downstream conductivity logger, with chloride values annotated at each node.",
  alt = "Box-and-arrow diagram of the flowpath from a deep parent fluid through degassing and discharge points to Steamboat Creek and a downstream logger.",
  id = "fig-conceptual"
```

The three independently sampled thermal points (fissure, resort tank, nearby well) give Na/K reservoir temperatures of 173.4, 179.2 and 180.2 C, a 6.8-degree range and a coefficient of variation of 2.1 percent. Three points are too few for a formal test, and I do not dress them up with a p-value. But a spread this tight, against the 50 to 100 C divergence between geothermometers and measured temperature across the full sample set, is consistent with these points sharing one deep source.

## A baseline chemical-evolution characterization of the flowpath

Everything here comes from the mixing, reaction-path and geothermometer runs above, with no new PHREEQC runs. The samples were all collected in one field season, so this is a one-time baseline: a demonstration that the approach can reconstruct mixing, chemical evolution and connectivity along a flowpath from a single snapshot. Tighter end-members, a paired uncertainty estimate for the inverse model and SBS_0001's unresolved tension are deferred to the same-day synoptic sampling round in the sampling plan.

The baseline does two things. It links the fissure geochemistry to the creek-scale proxy work, because the mixing fractions below are the quantitative bridge between them: both ask how far, and in what chemical form, the same thermal signal travels from its source. And it gives a chemical baseline for the Lower Sinter Terrace as it stood this season, after the 2025 eruption and while the terrace is still changing. Any new feature, including the hot spring found in August 2026, can be checked against the same framework: does it share the fissure's deep signature, and does it behave like a well or a spring near the surface?

**How much of each discharge point is fissure-strength fluid?** Using the chloride-based mixing fraction against the fissure and SBRR end-members (@fig-mixingfraction), the three springs and the seep sit at 0.77 to 0.89 (mostly fissure-strength fluid, modestly diluted), the nearby well SBW_0001 at 0.57, and the resort tank at 1.04, above the fissure reference, a finding and not an error. SBRR anchors the dilute end by definition, and SBBV, further down Steamboat Creek, still implies about 14 percent fissure-strength fluid by chloride, the same signal at much lower concentration that the 58.7 L/s thermal-discharge estimate is built on. The same conservative mixing framework therefore explains both the terrace and the creek. How that discharge compares with Sorey's earlier estimates is in the proxy chapter.

```{r fig-mixingfraction}
#| results: asis

  "output/figures/manuscript/mixing_fraction_by_target.png",
  "Chloride-based mixing fraction (fraction fissure end-member) for every downgradient target, colored by feature type.",
  alt = "Horizontal bar chart of mixing fraction for six targets, sorted from SBBV (lowest) to the resort tank (highest, exceeding 1).",
  id = "fig-mixingfraction"
)
```

```{r tbl-mixingfraction}
mix_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/mixing_fraction_summary_table.csv")
knitr::kable(
  mix_tbl, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Target", "Feature type", "Mixing fraction (fissure end-member)"),
  caption = "Chloride-based conservative-mixing fraction against the fissure (f=1) and SBRR (f=0) end-members, for every downgradient target, sorted low to high."

```

**What is gained or lost, species by species?** Comparing each target's chemistry with what its mixing fraction predicts if every species were conservative (@fig-gainloss), sodium is essentially conservative everywhere (within 6 percent), the direct justification for treating chloride and sodium as reliable tracers here. Potassium is modestly gained everywhere (13 to 31 percent), an open signal that may reflect mild clay or feldspar exchange. Sulfate and alkalinity separate the feature types (@fig-springswells). Every spring and the seep gain far more sulfate than either well (44 to 62 percent against -3 to 20 percent), and alkalinity is gained at both wells but lost at two of the three springs. Open springs and seeps are exposed to the atmosphere in a way a cased well is not, so oxidation of residual hydrogen sulfide to sulfate and loss of CO2 that would support alkalinity both have more opportunity before a sample is collected.

```{r fig-gainloss}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/species_gainloss_heatmap.png",
```

**Is the connection chemically feasible for every feature type?** @fig-tempprofile puts the three-stage cooling picture and the creek's re-warming between SBRR and SBBV side by side. The answer is neither a clean yes nor a clean no. The Na/K agreement (173 to 190 C across every thermal feature) is consistent with one shared deep source feeding wells, springs and the seep. But the sulfate, alkalinity and quartz-versus-measured-temperature patterns show that springs and wells differ systematically in near-surface process: springs and the seep cool further below their quartz temperature and gain sulfate and lose alkalinity in a way the wells do not. The defensible statement is that these features are consistent with a shared deep source but not with identical near-surface pathways. A proximity map cannot show that on its own, since SBS_0001 and SBW_0001 are only 109 m apart yet fit very differently.

```{r fig-tempprofile}
  id = "fig-tempprofile"
)
```

**A system still changing.** The terrace has kept changing since the 2026 poster. In August 2026 the author and Dave found a new seep-fed hot spring among bedrock boulders at a spot that had not been active before, and a nearby resident separately confirmed it was new. We returned on 27 September to photograph and GPS-log it (@fig-hotspring; times and coordinates are from camera EXIF data). The same day we noted a native-sulfur deposit that has visibly grown and looks fresh (@fig-sulfur) and a seep discharging from alluvium directly onto hard sinter bedrock (@fig-seep). The same seep was photographed on an earlier visit (@fig-seep-compare). Together these support the poster's conclusion that fluids are still redistributing within an existing shallow conduit system, and they are the reason the remapping and monitoring need to happen now.

# Further work: geophysics, a geologic model, and surface mapping {#sec-further}

The last chapter describes work that goes beyond this proposal but is already partly prepared. Electrical resistivity lines, if the Lower Terrace landowners give permission and Christopher Kratt of UNR can run them, would give the extent of the clay-altered cap and the depth of the fissure zone. A Leapfrog 3-D model of the wells, logs, faults and fissures would group samples by what they have flowed through and let the choice of reactions in the geochemical models rest on the rock. Surface mapping of the terrace, built from the thermal imagery and the mapped fissures, would tie these together in a Lower Terrace model.


## A geologic model and surface mapping of the Lower Terrace

The wells, logs, faults and fissures already in the database could be assembled in Leapfrog into a conceptual 3-D geologic model. Input files exist for 236 wells with collars, depths and elevations, plus lithology and the digitized fault and fissure traces, and every coordinate is in UTM zone 11N with elevations sampled from the 1 m lidar-derived elevation model. The purpose is limited. The model would group samples by what they have flowed through, so that mixing end-members and the reactions tested in PHREEQC rest on the rock, and it would show where the logged wells sit relative to faults and lithology. It is not a flow model, and no hydraulic properties are assigned, because none are measured at the resolution a flow model would need. Together with the thermal map and the mapped fissures, it would form the surface and shallow-subsurface model of the Lower Terrace that the chemistry in this thesis can be placed in. Full detail on the inputs and the scope limits is in Appendix A.

# Expected products

- A calibration equation relating chloride to specific conductance, or a set of site-specific equations, with stated uncertainty.
- A quantitative recommendation for the minimum sampling frequency needed for ongoing chloride monitoring at Steamboat.
- A PHREEQC-based physical justification (or documented limitation) for using specific conductance as a chloride proxy at this site.
- An updated interpretation of thermal-water discharge and conservative-tracer behavior before and after the 2025 eruption.
- Two candidate manuscripts: *Conductivity-Based Monitoring of Chloride Discharge at Steamboat Hills* (targeting *Geothermics* or *Geothermal Energy*), and *Hydrochemical Evolution of the Lower Sinter Terrace System Following the 2025 Eruption* (drawing on the PHREEQC, tracer-ratio and historical-comparison results above).
- A three-dimensional conceptual geologic framework for the monitored wells and springs, explicitly scoped as context rather than a flow model.
- A source by source map of surface heat and a resort-share estimate for the Lower Sinter Terrace, and a bounded Leapfrog compartment model used to group the chemistry.

# Conclusion

After the June 2025 eruption, the plain question at Steamboat is whether the system has a new source or an old one with a new outlet. Sorey and Colvard asked a version of it after the spring decline of the 1980s, and the 2026 poster written with Cary Lindsey asked it again from a handful of samples [@irvinlindsey2026]. The evidence there points to an old conduit reactivating, but it was gathered at poster speed. This proposal replaces that handful of samples with a method that can be repeated and whose uncertainty is stated.

The work will deliver three things. The first is a tested relation between specific conductance and chloride at two creek stations, with an error bound and a sampling interval no coarser than the data allow. If it holds across seasons, a cheap logger can supply most of the record that has so far had to be assembled from sparse chloride samples, and the thermal discharge of Steamboat Creek stops being a once-in-several-years estimate. The second is a source by source account of the Lower Sinter Terrace: where heat reaches the surface (488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius), which discharge points share the fissure's fluid, how much of the creek's thermal inflow is pumped from the resort well, and how the water changes chemically between the fissure and the creek. The third is a modest geologic frame, built from the wells, logs, faults and fissures already on file, that lets samples be grouped by what they have flowed through.

These results matter for different reasons to different readers. For the science, the 2025 eruption is the first event at Steamboat whose aftermath can be followed at this resolution, in a system with a 70-year discharge record to compare against, and a chloride-conductance proxy that works in thermal outflow would be useful at other geothermal systems where outflow is monitored by sampling. For regulators and operators, a calibrated proxy and a defensible sampling interval are a cheaper way to watch outflow than the current campaigns. For the owners of the Lower Terrace properties, the maps and the source attribution document what is changing and where.

The thesis does not claim to explain the cause of the reactivation. Whether changes in injection, regional groundwater, or the natural behavior of the conduit system were responsible needs operator data that this project does not hold, and the proposal says so where it matters. It does not build a flow model, and the thermal map, with its 44 degree ceiling and unrecorded flight date, supports attribution and area estimates rather than a heat budget. Each of these limits has a stated next step.

What holds the pieces together is that they are built to check one another. Chemistry, gas, thermal imaging, hydrology and time-series statistics share one database and one set of documented calculations, so that a conclusion reached one way, such as the gas geothermometer's reservoir temperature, can be tested against another, such as the water geothermometers or the chloride-based discharge. If the calibration holds, the same linkage lets each of those checks run continuously against a cheap sensor, and a one-time snapshot of Steamboat becomes a monitoring framework that whoever manages the system next can reuse. The 2026 logger record also calls for moving the loggers and measuring discharge by hand at the new sites, as described in the sampling plan. Until chloride samples overlap the loggers, the summer flux estimates in this proposal are bounds; the 1 May 2026 estimate is the one measured date.

# Appendix A: supporting analyses {.unnumbered}

These sections hold the detail behind the main chapters: the PHREEQC workflow, diagnostic checks, additional reaction-path targets, and the comparison with the 1986 to 1989 monitoring network. They are included for the committee and for anyone repeating the work.

## PHREEQC workflow in detail {.unnumbered}


Aqueous speciation and saturation-index modeling is run through the PHREEQC 3 executable [@phreeqc] (the standalone program, not an R reimplementation) against every sample with complete enough chemistry (404 samples as of this writing), with a thermodynamic database chosen per sample by temperature and total dissolved solids and a fallback when the first choice does not converge. This section describes which samples are modeled, how their chemistry is assembled and cleaned first, and what the output is used to decide.

**Sample eligibility.** A sample is modeled once it has pH, temperature and concentrations of chloride, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and alkalinity, the minimum a speciation calculation needs. Field pH and temperature are preferred over laboratory values, since a laboratory reading taken days after collection has drifted from in-situ conditions. Silica, sulfate, lithium, boron and a few trace metals are used when available but do not decide eligibility. A sample that does not qualify is logged with the field it is missing, so the gap between the samples that exist and those that are modeled stays visible.

**Assembling and cleaning the chemistry first.** Samples come from several sources spanning more than seventy years (field sampling, NDEP routine and public-records chemistry, and historical literature transcribed from Sorey and Colvard, Mariner and Janik, and Skalbeck), and the sources disagree on units and on how alkalinity is reported. Every concentration is converted to mg/L, and alkalinity reported as CaCO3 is converted to bicarbonate mass using the 61.02/50.05 equivalent-weight ratio (1.2189). This mattered: an earlier version left alkalinity out for one major source, which pushed the median charge-balance error from about 0.7 percent to a misleading 60 percent for the same samples. A bad charge balance should be checked as a data-handling problem before the chemistry is blamed.

**End-member grouping.** Samples with complete chemistry are assigned to a thermal end-member (outlet and thermal-well samples), mixed waters (a partial thermal signature) or dilute background waters, using the hydrochemical-facies clustering described below and cross-checked against PHREEQC's own fluid-type classification, not only the site-type label on file. This makes the conservative-tracer check and the Cl/B comparison below depend on chemistry and not on an arbitrary site-based split.

**Conservative-tracer evaluation.** Four ratios (Cl/B, Na/Cl, Li/Cl and SiO2/Cl) are tracked across the 1950s, the 1990s and the present to ask whether the thermal end-member's composition has stayed stable, independent of what a chloride-conductance calibration finds. A ratio that drifts through time or differs between eras is evidence about source-fluid stability (see the Cl/B result in @fig-clb below), and pooling the eras into one average would hide it.

**Mixing and inverse modeling.** A two end-member mixing fraction is computed from chloride, and a PHREEQC mixing step then combines the end-member solutions at that fraction and compares the predicted chemistry with the sample's, which tests the mixing hypothesis and is more than an arithmetic ratio. PHREEQC's inverse mode solves for mixing fractions and mineral mass transfer together within stated uncertainty bounds. One mixing run and several inverse runs exist. The first inverse run (target Soccer Field Monitoring Well, end-members samples 816 and 829) was once reported as finding one solution; that came from a parser reading PHREEQC's echoed input solutions as a result, and PHREEQC's own output says "Number of models found: 0." The parser was fixed on 2026-10-25. That run also used a representative, not time-paired, end-member pair, because no two chloride samples have yet been collected close enough in time, which is the gap the calibration sampling plan is meant to close. The inverse runs for the Lower Sinter Terrace targets, including the one that finds a solution only at 12 percent uncertainty, are described at the end of this appendix.

**Forward reaction-path titration.** Because the inverse models for the Lower Sinter Terrace find no solution at the standard uncertainty, a forward method was built. Two named end-members are mixed at a known conservative fraction, and a PHREEQC reaction step then moves one or more candidate mineral phases through net precipitation and net dissolution, comparing the modeled trajectory with the target sample at each step. It was also used to test two ideas for SBS_0001, whose chemistry (the highest sulfate and lowest alkalinity of its peer group) points away from a carbonate explanation: adding sulfate or fluoride phases, and substituting a higher-sulfate meteoric end-member. Results are reported below.

**Assumptions and limitations of the forward titration method.** Four limits bear on how much weight the results can carry. First, every phase supplied to a run is titrated by the same reaction-progress amount at each step, with no constraint that two phases dissolve or precipitate one to one. Second, one mixing fraction, computed from chloride, is held fixed during the titration, so a sample whose best explanation needs both a different fraction and a reaction could be mis-scored. Third, the fit compares modeled values with reported concentrations with no allowance for analytical error, so a sample within ordinary error of the model looks as wrong as one with a real discrepancy. Fourth, results depend on which phases are supplied: the sensitivity test on SBS_0001 below moves its best-fit error from 44.5 to 30.6 percent on phase and end-member choices alone. SBRR's role as a conservative, not pure, meteoric reference carries into every one of these tests.

**Interpretation framework.** Every PHREEQC run here answers one of three questions: whether the water types are chemically distinct, whether conductance behaves conservatively enough to stand in for chloride, and whether the thermal end-member's composition has held up over the seventy-year record. A result that bears on none of them is not reported.

**Chloride to boron ratio across seven decades.** A two-sample comparison of the curated thermal end-member (seven historical samples from Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992]; six modern samples from this project's field campaign) finds the ratio similar in size but not identical: 19.6 for 1950-1991 versus 21.9 for 2024-2026 (t = -2.92, 9.9 degrees of freedom, p = 0.015; @fig-clb). This is evidence against a wholesale change in source water. The small shift of roughly 12 percent could come from an analytical-method difference between eras or from a real geochemical change, and the proposed work is designed to help decide which.

```{r fig-clb}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/cl_b_ratio_by_era.png",
  "Chloride-to-boron ratio in thermal end-member samples, 1950-2026.",
  alt = "Scatter plot of chloride-to-boron ratio by well name, comparing 1950-1991 samples to 2024-2026 samples.",
  id = "fig-clb"
)
```

**Geothermometer divergence.** Sodium/potassium and quartz/chalcedony geothermometers applied to the same thermal samples diverge systematically: quartz sits below the measured discharge temperature and sodium/potassium above it (@fig-geo). That is the pattern expected for one cooling, diluting flow path from a reservoir of roughly 150-250 degrees Celsius, and not for two disconnected water types.

```{r fig-geo}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/geothermometer_comparison.png",
  "Geothermometer estimates versus measured discharge temperature, per-well mean across all thermal samples with complete chemistry.",
  alt = "Paired-point plot comparing sodium/potassium and quartz/chalcedony geothermometer temperature estimates to measured discharge temperature, per well.",
  id = "fig-geo"
)
```

**Are these samples equilibrated enough to trust Na/K at face value?** Every Na/K reservoir temperature in this proposal assumes the fluid reacted with its host rock long enough to approach equilibrium. A Giggenbach (1988) Na-K-square-root-Mg ternary built from the PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry of the seven flowpath samples tests that (@fig-giggenbach). The fissure and resort tank plot inside the Full Equilibrium field, the three springs and the seep in the Partial Equilibrium band, SBW_0001 just inside the Immature field, and SBRR (the dilute meteoric reference) at the magnesium-rich corner, where a cold, unreacted water belongs. This supports the Na/K estimates for the fissure, resort tank and springs, and cautions that SBW_0001's estimate is the least mature of the group.

```{r fig-giggenbach}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/giggenbach_ternary.png",
  "Giggenbach (1988) Na-K-sqrt(Mg) maturity ternary, PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry, all seven flowpath samples.",
  alt = "Na-K-square-root-Mg ternary diagram with seven labeled points against full equilibrium, partial equilibrium and immature water fields.",
  id = "fig-giggenbach"
)
```

**A second, independent water-type check.** A Cl-SO4-HCO3 ternary (Giggenbach 1991, @fig-anionternary) cross-checks the Piper diagram with a different scheme: all six thermal samples fall in the Mature Waters field and SBRR in Peripheral Waters near the bicarbonate corner, agreeing with the Piper diagram's separation of SBRR from the thermal cluster.

```{r fig-anionternary}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/anion_ternary.png",
  "Cl-SO4-HCO3 ternary (Giggenbach 1991), PHREEQC-conditioned chemistry, all seven flowpath samples.",
  alt = "Chloride-sulfate-bicarbonate ternary diagram with seven labeled points against mature, steam-heated and peripheral water fields.",
  id = "fig-anionternary"
)
```

**Does a multicomponent equilibrium exist, or only the quartz/chalcedony pair?** The quartz versus Na/K divergence compares two minerals at a time. A shared equilibration temperature (Reed and Spycher 1980) would show as several minerals' saturation indices crossing zero at about the same temperature, which can be checked in the stored 25-300 degree Celsius, 13-step temperature sweep for the six thermal samples with no new PHREEQC run. It does not appear (@fig-mineraleq). Quartz and chalcedony cross zero within roughly 15-50 degrees Celsius of each sample's measured discharge temperature, calcite and dolomite stay supersaturated across almost the whole range, and anhydrite and fluorite stay undersaturated throughout. At no sample do two or more minerals besides the quartz/chalcedony pair converge within 15 degrees Celsius of one another (@tbl-geotherm). That sharpens the quartz versus Na/K result: the apparent quartz/chalcedony agreement is not an artifact of checking only two minerals.

```{r fig-mineraleq}

show_fig(
  "output/figures/manuscript/mineral_equilibration.png",
  "Multicomponent mineral-equilibration diagram: saturation index vs. temperature for six candidate minerals at the six thermal samples plus SBBV (downstream creek, not itself thermal), from the stored PHREEQC_Temp_Sweep output.",
  alt = "Six-panel plot of saturation index versus temperature for six minerals, one panel per thermal sample, with a line at each measured temperature.",
  id = "fig-mineraleq"
)
```

```{r tbl-geotherm}
geo_tbl <- read.csv("data/derived/phreeqc/geothermometer_summary_table.csv")
geo_tbl$multicomponent_converges <- ifelse(geo_tbl$multicomponent_converges, "Yes", "No")
knitr::kable(
  geo_tbl[, c("location_name", "measured_temp_c", "T_NaK_gigg_C", "T_NaK_four_C",
              "T_quartz_C", "T_chalcedony_C", "multicomponent_converges")],
  digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Sample", "Measured T (C)", "Na/K (Giggenbach)", "Na/K (Fournier)",
                "Quartz", "Chalcedony", "2+ minerals converge?"),
  caption = "Geothermometer comparison, all eight flowpath samples including the downstream creek station SBBV, sorted by measured discharge temperature. The Na/K estimates at SBRR (256 C) and SBBV (197 C) are shown for completeness but are not physically meaningful at these dilute, non-thermal creek sites, consistent with the caveat stated elsewhere in this proposal. No sample shows two or more minerals besides quartz/chalcedony converging within 15 C of each other."

```

Including SBBV extends the picture one step downstream. Its quartz (64 C)
and chalcedony (45 C) equilibration temperatures sit between SBRR's (52 C
and 36 C) and the thermal features', while its measured temperature (23.7
C) is only about 8 C above SBRR's (15.2 C). Silica at SBBV therefore still
carries a faint thermal signature, in the same direction as its elevated
chloride, even though no mineral set converges on a shared equilibration
temperature there either (@fig-mineraleq). Its Na/K estimate, like
SBRR's, reflects dilute water and is not interpreted as a reservoir
temperature.


## Comparison of the 1986-89 monitoring network with the present {.unnumbered}


Collar's thesis [@collar1990thesis] documents the monitoring network in place when the main-terrace springs failed, and it is the closest yardstick for the one assembled here. In 1986 to 1989 the network was dense at the spring vents and in bedrock. It had water levels in about a dozen main- and low-terrace spring vents, in strat wells 2, 5, 9, 13 and 14, in GS-1, GS-8 and an old spa well on the low terrace, in OESI wells OW-1, OW-2 and IW-1, and in private alluvial wells (Steinhardt, Brown School, Herz 2, Pine Tree Ranch-1 and others), with chloride and boron at several of them, plus stream gaging at 63 stations. Today's network is denser in continuous temperature and conductance (a dozen temperature loggers, some since lost, and two conductivity loggers) and has modern laboratory chemistry and gas data. It has no current water level in the strat wells or the production reservoir and none at the spring vents, the two gaps Collar and Sorey and Colvard both said limited their conclusions. @tbl-oldnew puts recent values beside the older ones, with the comparability limit in each row.

The chloride comparison at the two logger reaches (@fig-collarcl) is the
clearest case. At Rhodes Road, Collar's two S10 values fall inside the NDEP
record, and this project's 2026 SBRR sample does too, so the upstream control
is chemically the same place it was in 1988-89. At Geiger Grade the NDEP
record is far more variable, from 10 to 760 mg/L, and Collar's three S70
values (130-418 mg/L) sit inside that scatter; because S70 carried only
0.1-3.7 cfs it may be a thermal side channel rather than the main creek, so
this match is provisional until Plate 4 is georeferenced. The discharge
comparison (@fig-discharge) needs more care than the chloride one. White's
1955 total of 1,125 gpm includes about 315 gpm from wells and is not
comparable with the creek-inflow values; only creek-inflow rows are plotted on
one axis, and Shump's value, made with specific conductivity, is labeled as
such. Applying this project's two-station flux difference to Collar's own
cleanest survey (S10 against S77, 4 March 1989) gives about 32 L/s (508
gpm), against his reach-summed 660 gpm (42 L/s) for the same date, so the
two-station method probably reads about a quarter low in a survey like that.
The 58.7 L/s database value and the 27 L/s poster value should be read with
that in mind.

Collar's spa-well observation also offers a test that can be run on current
data. If an intermittently pumped well near the low terrace produces a
weekday-weekend cycle in nearby heads, the resort-tank well (SBW_0002), which
is pumped intermittently by an air-lift, might leave a trace in the nearby
loggers. A weekday-weekend and seven-day spectral test on the daily mean
temperature of seven loggers (six terrace sites and SBRR, 83-98 days each, after removing a
15-day running mean) found none: weekend-minus-weekday differences were
within 0.9 C (the largest at the fissure logger), and no Kruskal-Wallis
test across weekdays had p below 0.7. Temperature is a weaker indicator than
the water levels Collar used, so this is a negative result for temperature
only; a pressure transducer in GS-1 or the resort-tank well would be the
direct equivalent.


## Hydrochemical endmember characterization {.unnumbered}


Following RQ1 and RQ3, every water sample with complete
major-ion chemistry (157 samples as of this writing) is assigned to a
hydrochemical facies using unsupervised clustering, cross-checked by
principal component analysis and an independent statistical classification
method, and compared against PHREEQC's own fluid-type classification. The
thermal end-member's chemistry (specifically its chloride to boron,
sodium to chloride, lithium to chloride, and silica to chloride ratios) is
then tracked across the 1950s, 1990s, and present eras to test whether the
source fluid's composition, and separately its modeled equilibrium state,
have remained stable over more than seventy years.

**Hydrochemical facies recover known geochemistry.** Clustering every
sample with complete major-ion chemistry, independently cross-checked by
principal component analysis and a classification method, recovers a pure
sodium-chloride thermal cluster, a dilute background-water cluster, and an
intermediate mixed cluster, without being told each sample's site type in
advance: three independent statistical approaches converging on the same
chemical structure, as shown in @fig-facies.

```{r fig-facies}
#| results: asis
show_fig(
  "output/figures/facies/facies_pca_biplot.png",
  "Principal-component biplot of major-ion chemistry, colored by persisted hydrochemical-facies cluster assignment.",
  alt = "Principal component biplot of major-ion chemistry, points colored by hydrochemical facies cluster, showing thermal, mixed, and background groups.",
  id = "fig-facies"
)
```
